subsubtopic: ELIMINATION OF SEX DISCRIMINATION IN PAY PRACTICES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On December 17, 1975 and again on February 5, 1976, the leader of the New Democratic Party raised in this House the question of the widening gap between women's and men's incomes and urged that the provision in the anti-inflation program for an exemption from the general guidelines to ensure the achievement of equality of the sexes with regard to income be made mandatory instead of optional.
Since the government has failed to take such action and since women in the Canadian labour force continue to be discriminated against in terms of their incomes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House instruct the government to take steps to implement on a mandatory basis the permissive clause in the anti-inflation program relating to the elimination of sex discrimination in pay practices.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
For some months now in the New York Times, as well as New York Review of Books, and recently in Time magazine, April 19, 1976 edition, it has been estimated that since the Communist victory in Cambodia last year, one half million Cambodians, or one tenth of the population, have died from political reprisals, disease or starvation under the Khmer Rouge.

That Canada's External Affairs Department bring this matter before the United Nations for open discussion.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON GUARANTEES REQUESTED BY MR. BOURASSA PRIOR TO PATRIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister.
During the weekend a Liberal party convention took place in Quebec City where Premier Bourassa dealt with three specific points, namely the patriation of the constitution, the Olympic Games and the common front in the province of Quebec.
As far as the constitution is concerned, Mr. Bourassa stated that he represented one fortieth of the total population in America and that he required guarantees by the Prime Minister of Canada before he agrees with the idea of partriating the constitution. Is the right hon. Prime Minister in a position to tell the House whether the guarantees required by Mr. Bourassa have been given to him?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON GUARANTEES REQUESTED BY MR. BOURASSA PRIOR TO PATRIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must point out that the idea of such guarantees was accepted not only by myself but also by the nine other provincial premiers at the meeting of first ministers in the month of April last when we got together to discuss this among other things. This was explained quite clearly in a letter tabled in the House before the Easter recess.
In brief, everyone is prepared to give guarantees so the French fact, so the French language may continue to exist on an equal basis in this country. That is the policy of the federal government, and of all parties in the House. There is no question about that. It is on the wording itself of a guarantee that there has been no agreement thus far. The hon. member no doubt learned from the papers tabled in the House that the federal government made an effort together with the province of Quebec to draft such a guarantee. Now, if the premier of the province of Quebec wants other formulas, or other clauses, I think it would be up to him to come up with proposals, otherwise he is asking in theory for something that was already given in theory.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL AID IN FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
About the constitution, as far as I was able to see last night, the premier of Quebec has not yet understood, but nevertheless he suggested that yesterday the President of the Treasury Board was meeting provincial Finance Minister Garneau about the Olympics and that an agreement was about to be passed whereby Ottawa would come to the help of the Montreal Olympic Organizing Committee which forecasts a very great deficit. Did the government suggest or propose to the federal government any assistance to fill that deficit that will occur in Montreal?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: FEDERAL AID IN FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the government on that has not changed for the last two years, and has still not changed in the past month. We supported the systems of self-financing from the start. I said on several occasions in the past two years that we would look at any reasonable system of selffinancing. I said in answer to the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont recently that that was still the position of the federal government.
I strongly refused and still refuse that money be taken out of the federal treasury to cover a deficit incurred by the Olympic Games Organization Committee, the city of Montreal or the province of Quebec, as regards the Olympic Games. This position remains unchanged. I think that the province of Quebec now understands such view and, if I am well informed, it is considering self-financing propositions, and that will be the end of those stories to the effect that the federal treasury will help make up the deficit incurred.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the question period I very briefly raised a point of order. I raise it again now in a little more detail and depth in order to get an answer, guideline, or possibly a ruling from Your Honour with regard to the whole question of ministerial responsibility and, indeed, the right of members of the opposition to question members on the treasury benches with respect to matters within their jurisdiction or, indeed, competence.
There has been a fair amount of circumlocution during the past few days and weeks with regard to the question whether there has been any vetting of contracts or dealings by a particular minister with regard to a particular province or region of Canada. In statements made today by the Prime Minister it came out that there has been input by a minister or group of ministers with regard to matters arising in various provinces. In other words, there has been an admission on the part of the government that at this point in time there is some responsibility attributable to certain ministers for matters arising within their areas. If, in fact, the government has given some responsibility with regard to granting of contracts or leases, and indeed the matter on which we are now questioning the government, the ministers involved in particular areas should be responsible for answering certain questions with regard to that.
If Your Honour in fact finds there is no requirement on the part of ministers to answer questions regarding matters arising within their general areas, or in fact it is not a matter of responsibility or places the legal interpretation that ministers have no right to have input with respect to contracts within a particular province or area, that is one thing. However, there has been no admission on the part of the government or the Prime Minister that this in fact goes against the Financial Administration Act: they say that the practices and procedures are quite within the law.
After admitting that they are vetting contracts and leases within a particular province, ministers should be obliged to answer questions with regard to their involvement and participation in them. If they have this responsibility, they should be required to answer in the House of Commons with regard to all aspects of their activities relating to the granting of contracts. They should not be allowed to hide behind the technical appellation they have with respect to a particular department, but should in fact answer questions regarding any input into the granting of contracts. I give as an example the fact that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did answer questions with respect to the involvement of his staff relating to matters over which he does not now have jurisdiction.
I submit to Your Honour, with the greatest deference, that it should not only be a ruling of the Chair but a right of opposition members to have every opportunity to investigate these matters, whether they be technically within the responsibility of a particular department, if-as it is now acknowledged-there is some method within cabinet for input by ministers for particular areas. I ask Your Honour to take this matter under consideration and in future question periods to allow us to direct questions to leaders within a particular province, as there is apparently an admission that they do in fact vet all contracts that come within their province.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: SALE OF STAMPS TO FOREIGN DISTRIBUTORS AT DISCOUNT- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is fairly obvious that there is a long-standing tradition in this place-and there are very good reasons for it-that a responsible minister answers in relation to matters having to do with his department and matters coming within his purview when matters cross several departments; and, of course, questions are from time to time put to the Prime Minister. It is perfectly obvious that members opposite may have questions of interest having to do with political matters or matters outside the purview of a minister's department or the government's operations as a government, but this House is not the place for those questions to be put. In fact, the rules of this House prohibit it.
There is, in each case to which the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar refers, where any matter of government business takes place, a minister responsible for that business, and-certainly in this government-he stands in his place ready to take responsibility for what is done within his department, to answer for it and to answer for the procedures in relation to it.
There are, of course, many submissions from members of parliament inside the House and citizens outside the House in relation to matters of government business. Indeed, conscientious members of the opposition from time to time write to ministers asking that careful consideration be given to a particular case or cause of a constituent, district or city. Clearly, that does not shift any responsibility from the member of the opposition but, rather, leaves responsibility on the government and the minister in relation to his department for the thing that is done, if it is done, and the way in which it is done. That supports the long-standing rule with regard to questions to ministers relating to their departments and the exception to it made in relation to the Prime Minister because of his broad, over-all government responsibility.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: SALE OF STAMPS TO FOREIGN DISTRIBUTORS AT DISCOUNT- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the acting government House leader referred to the opposition and our request for answers to certain questions. Indeed, the acting government House leader, the Minister of Transport, put the classic case within the rules of this House with regard to questions about ministerial responsibility as established by the government.
The questions that we are now asking have been responsibly and fully dealth by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar. They relate to a direct assignment of responsibility by the Prime Minister, the leader of the government, to particular ministers. One concerns the Minister of the Environment, at the time the minister of regional economic expansion, whose mandate from the leader of his party and the government went far beyond the operations of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. By the admission of the Prime Minister today-and it will be seen in public print tomorrow-the minister was involved in vetting things that had absolutely nothing to do with regional economic expansion. That was not by accident, but by design, because he was an acknowledged leader in a particular province. Surely it would be improper, and would indeed fetter the ordinary operations of the opposition, if the Chair allowed the government to hide behind the classic definition that was just put by the Minister of Transport, as it has no applica-

tion to this particular type of case. That is the point of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar.
I go one step further. If there is to be any order with respect to leasing, rentals or anything else involving government expenditure, something must govern-and surely that is the Financial Administration Act. If there is to be a case made for ministerial propriety, surely questions can be directed to the President of the Treasury Board with regard to financial administration. In fact, we should not be left there; we should not be stepped from asking questions of a minister whom we feel is carrying out responsibilities, as admitted by the Prime Minister, beyond the power of the ministry under the Financial Administration Act. Surely we cannot be fettered in that respect. That is the point made by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar, one which is important from the point of view of the opposition and its rights to ask questions and the responsibility, at least politically, of the government to answer them.
It is such an important question that I ask you, Mr. Speaker, not to make a judgment today but to consider the matter in light of what has been said on both sides and decide later whether it would be proper to fetter the opposition in this way.

subsubtopic: SALE OF STAMPS TO FOREIGN DISTRIBUTORS AT DISCOUNT- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to support the position taken by the Minister of Transport, the acting House leader, and to indicate, by using one or two examples, that his view is perfectly correct. The minister responsible for a department or for a particular appointment must, in the end, answer for it. I am answerable for appointments, for instance, when I name a particular person to the Senate from a province which is not my own province. I would, however, ask the advice of the senior member from that province.
When I appointed the former Conservative leader from Nova Scotia to the Senate a few months ago, I did discuss the matter with the Secretary of State for External Affairs who knows that province well and was in a position to confirm the respectability and qualifications of that particular person. When I named the former Conservative member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), to the Senate, I discussed the matter with the present Minister of the Environment because that is a province which he, also, knows well. But the responsibility of appointments to the Senate is mine, just as the opposition has been making it clear that I was responsible for appointing Senator Giguere. If they have questions to ask, they can direct them to me. But the convenience of consulting a minister who represents a particular province, whether the matter concerns the appointment of a senator or of a lieutenant-governor, of finding a qualified lawyer or an engineer able to do a job, cannot be underestimated since these are things a prime minister does not know because he cannot know the whole country.
It frequently happens that a minister responsible for a particular department is not acquainted with the firms which operate in another part of the country. I repeat, by way of example, that the responsibility is taken by the responsible minister and he is answerable to the House with respect to his political judgment. As the President of
April 26, 1976

the Treasury Board said, we are politicians; we have to make political judgments; we are answerable to the people for those judgments, and we are answerable to this House. If the opposition were to ask us, as they did ask the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, about Carmel Carriere, we would accept responsibility-and if the people do not like our answers, they know what to do at the next election.

Mr. Speaker, there is one thing that I would like to make very clear if I did not do so in the interview that I gave. I want the House to understand that there is no interference in the granting of contracts for which there is a call for tenders. The decision is based on the merits of the tenders. Even in the case of CARA which was the low bidder, this company got the Mirabel franchise instead of someone else.
When it is a matter of a recommendation where the government has some discretion, then representations come from everywhere. For instance, they can come from the New Democratic Party, from the Senate or from a
Ministerial Responsibility
judge, and there is nothing shocking about this. Everyone is aware of it, including the provincial governments and the opposition. Moreover, it is useless to create an atmosphere of scandal when we are simply following regular procedure.

subsubtopic: SALE OF STAMPS TO FOREIGN DISTRIBUTORS AT DISCOUNT- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, the minister-as is not infrequently the case-has added further confusion to the confusion which arose from his earlier statement. I believe he has an obligation to make a distinction between the kind of requests that he gets. In answer to questions on the orders of the day, he said, or implied, that members of the House of Commons made requests on behalf of their constituents or on behalf of other groups or persons in Canada. Such requests are, within one category, entirely appropriate; they form part of what we were elected to do.
What the minister failed to do when he spoke in a general way about requests was to distinguish those requests from requests which violate government guidelines or the laws of Canada. Such a distinction is important. If the minister has had requests made to him by any member of any party asking that a course of action be taken which violates treasury procedures or the laws of Canada, he has a duty to make available a list of such requests.

subsubtopic: SALE OF STAMPS TO FOREIGN DISTRIBUTORS AT DISCOUNT- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in complete agreement with the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). We should establish a distinction. For my part, I am not at all shocked when I receive requests from any source. Of course, the problem is as follows; when the request is for something illegal and unethical, I agree that it must be turned down; if undue influence is used, it should be criticized publicly. If the official opposition wants to blame us for such action, let them come right out and say so instead of making only general suggestions and creating an atmosphere of corruption where there is none.
If there has been, let them say where. As concerns the Sky Shops affair, I have cooperated entirely with the RCMP. I have given them all the information that they asked. I have given them everything that they wanted and they know this, including very personal documents. I have cooperated with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police because I knew that everything that I did was legal. I did nothing wrong in the Sky Shops affair.
The other matters are before the courts, and this is where they should be. If there are some irregularities, the judge will say so, and then we shall know where we stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: DRUG CASES IN COURTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
A close review of drug cases in the Courts of British Columbia was done prior to the end of 1975. As a result of this study, various steps have been taken in order to improve the prosecution of such cases. Legal supervision of the agents acting for the Attorney General of Canada in British Columbia has been decentralized and is now primarily the responsibility of the Regional Director of the Department of Justice in Vancouver. There exists in British Columbia a substantial back-log of cases of every nature. Discussions have taken place with representatives of the Attorney General of the Province in order to determine the possibility of improving court facilities in Vancouver for a better handling of drug cases. It is clear, however, that the back-log of drug cases in British Columbia is only part of a much larger problem of a back-log of criminal cases, not only in British Columbia but in other provinces as well. In February, the Minister of Justice asked the Law Reform Commission to accelerate its work in relation to pre-trial procedures with a view to reducing the delay in getting criminal cases on to trial. The Commission has agreed to do this and has established a task force consisting of judges, prosecutors and defence counsel to deal with this problem. The provincial attorneys general have all responded favourably and enthusiastically to this initiative and the Commission's proposals will be presented at a meeting of the eleven attorneys general in Vancouver in June. The Minister of Justice has stated that if general agreements can be reached about the changes which should be made, he would be prepared to move quickly with amendments to the Criminal Code.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
that Bill C-88, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

April 26, 1976
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House contains, essentially, two matters of interest and importance to the Wheat Board designated area. They are the formal provision of procedures for the election of the Wheat Board advisory committee; secondly, the broadening of the scope of the Canadian Wheat Board to establish separate pools for selected types of grain within an identifiable grade. This will be known to most members as a malting barley pool amendment, though in its words and possibilities it is broader than that.
The first part of the bill having to do with the election of the advisory committee follows an experiment which was very well received by the grain producers. The experiment was to set up an election procedure which allowed the producers within the Wheat Board area to nominate, and then to vote upon and elect, the members who would serve on their behalf on the 11-member Canadian Wheat Board advisory committee. There was a great deal of interest in the election that took place, in terms of the number of candidates and the breadth of experience and interest that the candidates represented, which resulted in electing members who in this way directly represent the producers in particular and identifiable regions. Under the existing law, of course, the election was a forerunner to the appointment by order in council since the law requires the 11-member board to be appointed in this fashion.
We had, of course, indicated that the election would be followed up with such appointment, and that has taken place. Indeed, the new committee has been functioning for a good number of meetings now, and while admittedly having some interesting growing pains as it became established, I think hon. members will agree that it is showing its real value. The Canadian Wheat Board relies on the committee for comment and opinion on matters affecting producers, though not, of course, transferring to it any of the essential responsibility for providing the best marketing expertise that the Wheat Board must exercise on its own. The advisory committee will, I hope play an increasingly important role in advising the Canadian Wheat Board of the views of producers on a multitude of matters and will also increasingly be in a position to report back to producers on matters within the board's responsibility. In this way producers can become informed by their own representatives in addition to the more formal releases or methods of communication adopted by the Wheat Board.
I said that the procedure was generally very well welcomed, and I believe that is also true of its operation. I am sure members will be glad of an opportunity in committee to look at the specific nature of the advisory board and to comment further upon it for its own future development. Certainly for my own part I shall welcome expressions of view from hon. members concerning the direction in which the advisory committee should go and the extent to which the input of producers can be improved. I have always been very concerned to establish as many means of consultation as possible with producers, particularly in regard to matters such as the marketing of their own grain in which they have a prime interest, even though necessarily it falls under the broad umbrella of the legislation of this parliament.
The establishment of a separate pool for malting barley has been discussed by those who have grown barley for quite a number of years. However, for a long time the view was taken by a good number of producer representatives that a pool was undesirable in view of the fact that the

selection of specific barley from among all the grades might be seen in itself as somewhat fortuitous and a rather special break for the individual producer who managed to have his grain selected.
As the selection of barley for a purpose such as malting became more important, and as more and more producers attempted to arrange their farm practices to raise a malting barley, putting increasing efforts into the production of barley for specific selection, the pendulum began to swing in the other direction. In the course of the years 1973 and 1974, therefore, we began to receive an increasing number of representations in favour of allowing for the separate pooling of the selected barley within a particular grade, and in due course the Wheat Board and its advisory committee joined in the representations that were made that this was a worth-while thing.
Accordingly, I indicated that I would be willing to put before the House a bill along these lines in the hope that the House would see fit to bring it into law in order for it to be effective in the present crop year. The indication of my willingness to do this came during the course of the last crop year when I indicated to the Canadian Wheat Board it would be desirable for it to keep accounts in such a way that if parliament did, indeed, make this law effective, the barley selected for malting this year could be pooled separately.
Hon. members from the Wheat Board region will be particularly aware of the fact that last year emphasis was placed on the desirability of separate pooling of selected grades of barley for malting purposes. In the last year period a good amount of what otherwise would be No. 1 feed barley was selected for malting purposes. Because the Wheat Board could not, under existing law, segregate the results of the pooling of that selected barley, it was merged with the broad pool for feed barley. While the difference between selected barley when it is selected from other higher grades is perhaps significant enough, it is even more significant in the case of selection from No. 1 feed barley. Quite obviously, as a result those farmers whose barley was selected felt they should have had the benefit of that selection. The argument could rage on, but certainly at this point in time many producer organizations-indeed, I do not know of an exception-have changed their former position in recommending against separate pooling and now endorse the separation of the selected grades.
As hon. members will know, I have been speaking about malting barley, and this is the key selection of grade that we have in mind; but the bill is broader, to give the Canadian Wheat Board and its advisory committee rather additional flexibility from time to time, when other types of grain within a broad grade are selected, to establish separate pools in those cases as well. I do not suggest the judgments will be easy in every case, as it was not over a period of years in this instance. However, it does seem to me it would be better to be in a position to respond quickly on the advice of producer groups, the advisory committee and of the Canadian Wheat Board itself, when a broad grade is being subdivided in practice by selection for a particular purpose, to allow pooling in that situation.
I therefore commend to hon. members this change in the legislation. I would be very glad to go into the reactions and views of the various representative groups throughout the prairie region with hon. members. I know their familiarity with these views will lead them to lending their support to this bill. I certainly welcome that as we see
April 26, 1976

it moving toward becoming law. In closing, I emphasize the importance of moving it forward since the crop year is moving along and it would be useful to add certainty to the proposition which I have put forward, that it would be desirable to have this law applied to the crop year now in progress, that is to say, the one which commenced last August 1 and which ends next July 31.
Notice of the intention to present the bill was given to the public well in advance of that time and I believe, therefore, that hon. members can move forward with happy hearts so that selected barley in this year can indeed be segregated in the pool, the Wheat Board having kept the appropriate accounts for that purpose.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore take great pleasure in moving the second reading of this bill and its reference to the committee.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister quite rightly pointed out that the experiment of an elected Canadian Wheat Board advisory committee has worked out well. I wish that committee the best in years to come. Bill C-88, as the minister has said, proposes to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act to provide for the establishment of separate pools for selected grains, such as malting barley, probably the selected oats going into the rolled oats trade, and we are hopeful it will also include payments for selected high protein grains.
I note that the Palliser Wheat Growers Association has written the minister suggesting that Bill C-88 presently before the House is the proper vehicle under which to sort out high protein grades. The association goes on to state that this would not require special binning at the country elevator level, but that the protein level could be determined as it is by our American friends. The association further states that the Canadian Wheat Board has received some 34 cents a bushel premium for 13.5 per cent protein wheat, compared with 11.5 per cent. It suggests it would seem only fair that farmers growing the higher protein should be compensated, thereby promoting this incentive. The association goes on to say that this would lead to better land utilization by producers in consistently low protein areas, improving their performance by growing higher yield varieties. The association ends its letter by stating:
Due to the frustrations from delays, the producers are ready for some action.
I hope we can look forward to protein being included under this bill. The bill also provides a permanent basis for the election of prairie grain producers to the Canadian Wheat Board advisory committee. Under the amendment, the board will exercise direction and supervision over the administrative process in all future elections to this advisory committee. The governor in council, however, will enact all rules and regulations, which means the minister will in fact have complete control. This will probably give producers some cause to ponder.
Mention could be made of the present snarl-up in the western grain stabilization plan whereby every producer now delivering must have the 2 per cent deduction applied, whether he wants to come into the plan or not, because the excluding stickers for their permit books are not yet available. This has caused the farmers in my area to become
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) even more skeptical of this plan, especially now that they find the government's contribution to the plan will only be a bookkeeping entry and the money will probably be used elsewhere. This money could, of course, be used to promote the metrication of our grain industry. This is incomprehensible to producers in southern Saskatchewan. We have had no estimate of the cost of this metrication plan, but we note United States publications claiming an estimate ranging from $40 million to $100 million for the switch in that great country. If we take one-tenth of that, we end up with something between $4 million and $10 million.
It is all right for the government to be promoting this program. The bureaucrats may well say, "Let the costs fall where they may." They are not in the business, of course, and do not have to buy new scales, new tools and new labels. It is impossible to understand the claims by metric commission officials that the conversion will increase the export of our grain as our grain is presently sold on the basis of metric tons. The United States has used more common sense in its conversion, which is more gradual and selective. Each move must pass the test of benefit and existing cost. I suggest we could well take a look at this method in our country.
Because of this forced 2 per cent deduction under the grain plan, farmers are properly asking whether the government is trying to force a signing-up. Producers rightly suggest that it is probably much easier to have the amendments made to the plan now than getting the plan established and then trying to have it amended.
The minister indicated there was some skepticism in years gone by about obtaining additional premiums for malting barley because it might appear that this is special treatment for those who produce malting barley. This a very tricky question. The domestic and export malting industries require barley that is relatively plump and uniform in size, true to variety and type, which does not have excessive amounts of physical imperfections.
It is absolutely imperative that uniform germination takes pl^ce in the malting process. Barley must be low in moisture content. If it has to be stored for long periods, artificial drying will adversely affect germination. Producers, further, have to use sound methods of threshing and be careful not to peel or break the kernels. The protein content is very important. Low protein content is desirable. Most of these requirements are above and beyond requirements in respect of grade.
I hope this will give some appreciation of the care and technique required by producers to have their barley rated malting. It is interesting that sales in this crop year to date, of some 274,000 bushels of malting barley, have been selected from grain company stocks. I hope there will be some assurance from the minister that the grain companies will not reap the benefits from the malting premium.
In the last full crop year-that is, the 1974-75 crop year- over 18 million bushels of feed barley ended up in the malting houses. When a producer delivers grain to a western country elevator, normally no official grade is placed on the grain. The ticket is simply marked "Graded by agreement". This is the official basis for payment if accepted by the producer. This was the basis for any final

April 26, 1976
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
payment by the Canadian Wheat Board. So any barley graded No. 1 feed and eventually ending up in the malt-house generated a final payment to the farmer of about 18 cents a bushel last year, whereas it generated a premium of up to and over $1 a bushel for the Canadian Wheat Board.
The minister is always saying he is held up by some final legal interpretation when it comes to giving the producer the benefit of the doubt. However, there seems to be no such qualms when the shoe is on the other foot. I think of the sorry story of the Temporary Wheat reserves Act payments of several years ago when producers were required to initiate court action in order to get the money from the government that was legally owing to them.
I question the legality of the Canadian Wheat Board proposal to pay to the grain companies some $10 million of the farmers' money in order to encourage the companies to build additional storage at Vancouver. All we know about this is what is reported in the Western Producer of April 15 where it is stated that the Canadian Wheat Board proposes to establish three categories. The companies were to receive guaranteed storage payments on 95 per cent of their total licensed capacity, less whatever percentage they reserved for non-board grain.
Those companies which build or increase their terminal elevator facilities by more than 2.5 million bushels will be eligible to receive guaranteed storage payments on all their licensed capacity. As I have said, it appears to me that this will cost western farmers some $10 million. I think the government of Canada could well take a look at this because it has a responsibility to help increase the storage space at the Pacific seaboard.
On top of that, the farmers are now aware of the proposed non-funding by the government under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. This, to them, seems to be consistent with the minister's mode of operation. We had a plea from him this year for more seeded acreage, and at the same time we had an announcement of lower initial grain prices to the western farmer. Our western grain, industry was built and developed on policies that were designed to bring the greatest good to the greatest number. We had standard handling tariffs. Now we have variable or flexible tariffs in country elevators.
We had no trucking from country elevators, but now we have it. We had standard grades across the prairies, and now we have protein standards at export and proposed protein granding at country elevators. We used to have the standard Crowsnest Pass freight rates for export grain. Now the minister is bringing forward proposals that the producers feel will make those rates variable. Where we formerly had complete Canadian Wheat Board control, we now have open market feed grains and a general freeing-up.
Grain from the northern and southern parts of the prairies used to be blended at export to give a uniform grade. Now the northern and southern grains are kept separate because of protein standards. Our whole grain transportation system, of course, is in a turmoil. The elevator companies do not know what the future holds. The railways do not know where they will go. Surely the government's transportation policy should be to develop a system to serve the needs of the grain industry, and not vice versa.

The net result of the meddling by the minister has brought the western grain industry to the point where it would be impossible to export the volumes of wheat of some 14 years ago. It is interesting to note that up to the present our wheat and Durum exports amount to some 260 million bushels. There are three more months until the end of the crop year. This means we will probably end up, at best, with 400 million bushels of wheat. Government grain statistics show that in the peak year, 1963-64, wheat exports were 594 million bushels. We might compare that with the 400 million bushels we will probably export this year in spite of all the government money poured into our system.
The minister has done this by using the capital accumulated by the discipline of the past. The word I get from the producers is, "Get the government off our backs for a while". By "the government," they mean the minister. No other country has the control of licensed varieties that Canada has. This is certainly necessary if we are to keep promoting our malting barley. It seems to me that we are slipping badly now. Our research scientists are being neglected. Their work on new varieties is being curtailed. Canada is losing its leadership.
Surely it is time for the government to allow producers to set up a check-off system so they can promote their own research and marketing. This could be done, hopefully, under the amendments we are now discussing in Bill C-88. We might look at our competitors in other countries to see what they are doing. We see that in Brazil they are expanding the network of paved roads to 63,000 kilometres. They will be spending $3.5 billion on railways in the period 1974-79. By the end of the decade the Brazilian merchant fleet will reach over 9'A million tons dead weight, with most of the ships having been produced in Brazilian shipyards.
On the other hand, we in Canada have practically no merchant marine. The rural credit programs in Brazil totalled $12 billion, with an average 11.2 per cent nominal interest rate, which in an inflationary economy means a real transfer to the agricultural sector. In our country, the largest grain handling organization, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, states its concern about the limited funds available and the lack of encouragement for young people to become involved in agricultural research and plant breeding. I should like to quote a statement by Mr. Avery Sahl, pool director and Wheat Board advisory committee member. He said:
But during the course of this discussion-and I might say that we had a Dr. Jack Morrison from Research Ottawa in attendance and I've personally had some communication with Dr. Hurd at the research station in Swift Current and some pretty startling realities have come to light as a result of those discussions ...
For instance, we've only got 30 cereal scientists or plant breeders left in Canada. They have about 29 or 30 back-up people such as chemists, you know, assist them in their efforts but I should also say that these same people, these same 30 plant breeders, really can't devote their total efforts to plant breeding because they're involved in teaching at universities and other administrative work.
He concluded by saying:
Well that's certainly true. During our discussion we learned that the people that are in the plant breeding program are in the general age
April 26, 1976

group of 50 years of age and we'll be losing these valuable people through normal retirement, you know, before very long.
The director says that the federal government has some responsibility in the area of basic research, as do agricultural producers through the Canadian Wheat Board, farmer-owned co-operatives and marketing agencies. So I say again that provision should be made in this bill for producer check-off as their contribution to the basic research that we need.
We are all aware of the fact that the Canadian National Railways' main line has been out of commission to the Pacific seaboard for some months. It is back in business now. The government has made no move to bypass this bottleneck in the Fraser canyon, which could be done with a simple 40-mile loop. We desperately need more facilities in the Pacific seaboard, and we see no reason why the government cannot act and why it cannot pay interest on the deferred settlements and extend those deferred settlements with interest for the present year or for two or three years.
We heard the minister say that we have to accept the "user pay" proposition and that the St. Lawrence Seaway tolls have to go up. It seems to me that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the free market system under which the users pay is not working for the general good. We are told that the AT and east rates for export flour and winter grains for the maritimes will be removed. In this particular case there was no prior consultation with the industries. It was an arbitrary decision by the minister playing fast and loose with the industry, I suggest. From 1954 to 1974 world demand for flour increased by 50 per cent. Canada's share of the flour trade declined from 31 per cent to 11 per cent in 1974. The world flour market is fiercely competitive due to the implementation of subsidy programs by many foreign governments. Many markets for our winter exports can only be met by the export of flour to West Africa and the West Indies where there is no milling capacity. The Soviet Union has indicated that Canada is no longer competitive in world flour markets and that further increases in price will require them to look for alternate suppliers.
To return to the matter of the AT and east freight rates, the removal of which will be disastrous for our flour industry, Mr. Sneath, president of the Manitoba pool elevators, had this to say:
We have stated many times that the Seaway provides a service which is in the national interest and should not, therefore, be expected to generate a profit. Approximately one year ago, it was suggested by the Seaway authority to the Hon. Jean Marchand, then minister of transport, that rate increases should be considered. At the same time, a proposal to write off the long-term debt and interest charges, was also suggested. We encourage the latter, and suggest that such a move would increase traffic and, even at present rates, keep the Seaway down in the black.
The Manitoba pool president stated that decisions on this matter should not be made arbitrarily. He said:
As a member of the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association, and as users of the Seaway, we feel strongly that Canadian users should be consulted about the effects of any increase in rates on their operations.
It does not take much studying of the western Canadian grain industry to realize that the minister has handed to Mr. Justice Emmett Hall the impossible task of deciding
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) the fate of our western rail system, primarily because none of the factors in our grain system at present are stable; everything seems to be in a state of flux. I will mention just one factor, namely, the inland terminal concept in western Canada which has everyone wondering.
The minister's treatment of our grain industry can be likened to a building catching fire. It is the combustion of one object which generates the heat required to ignite the next, and unless counter measures are taken the fire spreads farther and farther, becoming more difficult to control, until nothing is left.
When we look at the problems facing our industry, we remember that under the 1974 tariff structure for the country elevators it costs as much to lift the grain 50 feet into the air as it costs the railways to move it 1,000 miles. Other problems are the export grain rates to be changed, rail line abandonment, the metric conversion of the grain industry, the fact that our competitors have long-term deals with our best customers while we have none, more storage at the Pacific seaboard, etc. Perhaps we should consider storage of grain overseas where the customers are. Companies such as Imperial Oil, Standard Oil and Gulf would not keep their oil in the United States. They promote its sale by having it where the customers are. As I have mentioned, we need more research into new varieties of grain.
The minister's actions can be likened to baloney being sliced one thin slice after another. Pretty soon all we will have left is the string, and that is not much good to anyone. Right now grain farmers are about the only Canadian industry not priced out of world markets, and we would like to keep it that way.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my party generally supports this legislation in principle, but we have some comments to make on it. I hope the minister will consider some suggestions that we have to make both at this stage of the debate and in the committee for changes in the legislation. First I should like to comment on the bill in general, and then on two or three specific matters relating to it.
This bill defines the structure of the advisory committee, how its members will be elected, what their duties will be, how they will receive their pay and expenses, and so forth. The previous practice was that advisory committee members were appointed by the minister, usually on the recommendation of major farm organizations. As the minister explained earlier, and as we all know, the situation is now changed so that the producers themselves directly elect members of the advisory committee. The legislation also allows for the establishment of various constituencies for each of the 11 members of the committee and sets out the means for arriving at their pay, the meetings to be held- there will be six in number each year, and I will comment on that later-and who has authority to call a meeting.
One of the disturbing aspects of the situation is that no provision is made, either explicit or implied, for committee members to hold such meetings as may be necessary in order to report back to the permit holders who elected them. Previously there was a six-man advisory committee and the members were nominated by the western co-operatives and the farmers' union. It was not mandatory under

April 26, 1976
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) the act that they be selected in this manner but that was the practice followed, and it was possible under those circumstances for the members of the former committee to have a means of reporting back to the producers. All the members of the advisory committee were elected officers of farm organizations which were controlled by the producers. A method of reporting to farmers and bringing forward information respecting producers' opinions to the minister or the administrators of the Wheat Board was established.
The advisory committee members who will be elected under the new procedure may not be attached to farm organizations in an official capacity, and since they are nominated and elected we submit that provision should be made for them to be responsible directly to the producers in all respects. It seems to us that if the new committee is to function effectively, there must be provision for it to have the ability to report back to its constituents in the same way as a member of parliament. There must be provision for members of the committee to hold meetings and contact directly the individual producer or collectively contact producers in the regions they represent in the Wheat Board area.
It should also be possible for farmers in the constituency to initiate meetings if the need should arise and if they wish to meet with a member of the advisory committee. There should also be provision for the advisory committee to have a meeting called upon its own request. Provision should be made whereby the advisory committee, either unanimously or by a quorum of five or six members, could request the board to call a meeting of the committee. It should then be obligatory for the board to do so.
The legislation provides that the board shall call six meetings per year of the advisory committee. What would happen if some matter arose which members of the advisory committee thought was so urgent and important that an extra meeting was required? It seems to us that the advisory committee, through either a majority or a quorum, should be able to request a meeting, and that it should be obligatory on the chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board to call such a meeting. It should not be left just to the board or just to the limitation of the act providing for six meetings per year. If the members of the advisory committee feel there should be three or four meetings more than that during the course of a year, the legislation should allow it to happen. It should not be just at the whim of the minister or the Canadian Wheat Board.
If a majority of the advisory committee members feel that additional meetings are warranted, this bill should make provision for that and the members should be paid their pay and allowances. The committee should not be put in the position of being suspected of being nothing more than a puppet for the minister in charge of the Wheat Board or being at the beck and call of the Canadian Wheat Board. Some degree of autonomy and freedom of action of the advisory committee should be in the legislation. Unless something of this nature is provided for the committee, it will look too much like some sort of pussy cat for the board.

The bill proposes to amend section 10 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act and it lays out in full detail how the advisory committee shall be elected, how it shall be constituted, and so forth. It is to be constituted by regions, or what I choose to call constituencies, which each advisory board member will represent. The legislation provides that this shall be arrived at by the governor in council. I wonder why this could not be done by the redistribution commissioner who works on the boundaries of federal constituencies for members of parliament. Why cannot this be done by the redistribution commissioner, or at least by the Canadian Wheat Board itself? I ask that because, frankly, I would feel nervous if the decision as to the areas which members of the advisory committee will represent were left in the hands of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and his cabinet colleagues. I think I have good reason for that nervousness. I do not see why the governor in council should be the body to have responsibility for determining the boundaries of the constituencies of the members of the advisory committee.
The expenses and allowances paid to members of the advisory committee should be sufficient to allow them to incur what could be considered reasonable costs for travelling about the constituencies they represent, holding meetings and reporting back to their constituents, the grain producers who are the permit holders they represent. It seems to us that this should be a two-way street of communication, not only from the bottom up but from the top down. The advisory committee should be able to report back to those permit holders who are grain producers and tell them how much of their advice is being taken by the Canadian Wheat Board, by the minister or by both of them, and how much of it is being ignored. I submit that the grain producers have a right to know just what effect the advice of the advisory committee will have on the minister and the Canadian Wheat Board.
Having an advisory committee democratically elected by grain producers will be of little use if the grain producers have no way of knowing whether that committee is of any benefit to them, or whether the minister or the Canadian Wheat Board is paying any attention to it. Is this just going to be window-dressing, something which makes it appear as if the Canadian Wheat Board is drawing upon the best possible advice from the grain producers' representatives and using it? This two-way communication should be built into the legislation, which means allowing each member of the advisory committee sufficient expenses in order to report back to the grain producers he represents.
The legislation also provides for the continuing of grain deliveries from an existing crop year into a new crop year. There is nothing new about this. The minister is just making it formally possible in the legislation, but in many previous crop years the Canadian Wheat Board, grain companies, railroads and everyone just turned a blind eye. We always had a saying that July 31 could be a very long day. Quota deliveries for the previous crop year were delivered on the fourth, fifth, tenth and twenty-fourth days of the new crop year, but the storage tickets, or the cash tickets which the elevator agent made out were all dated July 31. This was to allow producers who, through no fault of their own, had been unable to deliver their quotas before the expiration of the crop year, to deliver them so that all
April 26, 1976

would be fairly treated. I hope that is the intent of the minister in putting this provision into the legislation.
The third change is a proposal to amend the act by bringing in an addition after section 32. Under the provisions of the new legislation, the Board could select certain grades, a minimum of two, and form a separate pool in any crop year. The purpose of this is to permit the setting up of separate pools for malting barleys so that the premiums now paid can be passed directly to the producers. This proposal also provides for the setting up of separate pools for separate classes of wheat such as Durum and winter wheat. We generally support that idea. However, I want to caution the minister and the House that while we support the idea of separate pools in the case of malting barleys and in some instances two or more grades of wheat, I hope the minister and the board will not allow this separate pooling to be carried on to such an extent that one of the major reasons for the existence of the Canadian Wheat Board is rendered useless.
One of the reasons for having a Wheat Board was that returns from the sale of grains would be pooled so that all producers would benefit relatively equally. Another reason was that bad weather or poor export markets would not cause one group of producers in any part of the Wheat Board area to be treated less fairly than those in another part of the Wheat Board area. I wonder whether the allowing of separate pooling for not less than two grades should be made something like not less than three grades. I wonder if this would prevent any narrowing down or pooling just for special areas which, I submit, could then weaken one of the main principles behind having the Wheat Board. The idea of doing this with malting barley is good, although I am concerned about the two-grade limit. That ought to be the minimum limit, otherwise we could destroy the very purpose for the existence of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Something which has happened in connection with malting barley in the last two crop years, and possibly before then, concerns me greatly. I am thinking of producers who have special permits to deliver carload lots of malting barley. Sometimes the Canadian Wheat Board or a grain company will phone a producer with a special permit for a carload lot of malting barley and ask him to deliver, but that producer must haul to another shipping point on another railway line because the railway company has abandoned temporarily the railway line serving him.
That has been the experience of hundreds of producers in the past two crop years. It happened in my own constituency before Christmas. The railway had shut down one line for over a month and announced it would not open it for two more months. Several producers within the area had carload lots which had to be delivered by December 20. But there were no trains. Consequently, the farmers were told to haul the grain an extra 20 or 40 miles one way. The extra trucking cost gobbled up any premium they might have earned from their malting barley. There is not much point establishing a separate pool for malting barley if in hundreds of cases the premium the farmer would earn from delivering a carload lot of malting barley is used to meet extra trucking costs, costs incurred because the rail line is not functioning.
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
If this is allowed to continue there will not be much in the pool to divide among farmers. It has happened in dozens of instances all over the three prairie provinces. The railways have allowed their railway lines to deteriorate. The rail lines are in a disgraceful condition. Trains have not run over some of them for months on end. Then, when a grain producer receives an order or a special order of the kind I have mentioned, he cannot ship from his own shipping point. Consequently, many Canadian Wheat Board shipping orders are left unfilled and the efficiency of the Canadian Wheat Board, the pool system, the block system, unit trains, etc., is effectively harmed.
In my constituency there is a line which had not carried a train for over three months. The railway had allowed the condition of the line to deteriorate. Many producers served by that line could not fill outstanding Canadian Wheat Board shipping orders. There were a number of carload lots of malting barley and odd carload orders for commodities such as rapeseed which could not be shipped by rail. There were over 200 outstanding regular Wheat Board shipping orders. In other words, five or six trainloads of orders could not be filled because that line was not operating.
The railway company would not run a train over the line in the winter. When the matter was raised with the minister and his officials, they said that winter is not a good time to run trains because there is a lot of snow. I point out that last winter was not a hard winter and the line could have stayed open. Not enough snow fell to block a gopher hole, let alone the railway track. The government used snow as an excuse. That was the reason for not running a train on a line about 120 miles long.
It should be pointed out to the minister, since he was involved with this, that if the ground under the track is in bad condition and if your rails are weak because the ties and rails have been insufficiently maintained, the time to run trains on that track is in winter when the ground is frozen. But no, the CPR had to have its own way. The railway closed the line for three or four months because, allegedly, it was snow-covered. So no trains ran over it in the winter months. But the line was also closed in the spring because the ground was soft. You end up with trains not running on branch lines until May or even mid-June. Sometimes people served by branch lines do not see a train on the line for as long as six months.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) suggested that an impossible task has been handed to Mr. Justice Hall. That is perfectly true. I do not know why the task was given to him in the first place. The railway companies should not have been allowed to abandon any rail lines. They should have been told that they will not be allowed to abandon any line until the facts are ascertained and Mr. Justice Hall advises or rules that a certain line can be closed. As I say, it should be the commission's task to decide whether, and which, rail lines should be abandoned. The commission will have an awkward task deciding if a rail line should be abandoned as the railway companies can argue that certain rail lines are already abandoned, so to speak, up to four months each year. The railways have allowed lines to deteriorate so much that they can argue, justifiably, that it is economic suicide to repair them, even if the commission decides to keep them open. The costs will seem horrendous to the
12872

April 26, 1976
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) railways and to the minister, and the government could well choose to ignore the recommendations of the Hall commission.
We submit that the legislation ought to be broader. Let me repeat something my party has been saying since 1935. Of course we shall argue for improved provisions when the bill is considered in committee. The bill ought to contain provisions which will broaden and strengthen the responsibility of the Canadian Wheat Board. All parties in this House support the existence in principle of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is like motherhood; nobody dares oppose the existence of the Canadian Wheat Board. But certain things done have tended to weaken the authority of the board and lessen its importance and strength.
We want the legislation to give the Canadian Wheat Board full jurisdiction over feed grains. The minister may argue that the farmer should be free to decide where to sell, that is, whether to sell on the open market or to the Canadian Wheat Board. To that I say that the farmers have over-whelmingly shown how they choose. Little feed grain is delivered and sold on the open market. That speaks well for the almost unanimous support western grain producers have shown for the Canadian Wheat Board. Their choice answers the contentions of those who want to cling to the outdated and outmoded free market concept in feed grains. I do not see why we should pander to them. We believe that full jurisdiction over feed grains should be returned to the Canadian Wheat Board. This piddling around with small lots of feed grain on the open market is of no benefit to most grain producers of western Canada.
I say that we should broaden and strengthen the responsibilities of the Wheat Board. This bill ought to do something we have advocated since the early 1930s, that is, put all grains under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. This means bringing commodities like flax, rye and rapeseed under the board's jurisdiction so that no significant quantities of grain in Canada are left to the whim of the grain speculators and the so-called open markets of Chicago, Minneapolis, Omaha, Winnipeg, and so on. In short, the Canadian Wheat Board should be the sole agency for dealing with all grains produced by western Canadian farmers. Farm organizations have been urging this for decades, as have certain members of parliament. But the government continues to ignore us. We say that this bill should bring under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board flax, rye and rapeseed. We will continue to fight for that.
In summary, when the bill gets to committee I ask the minister to make provision that whenever a quorum or majority of the advisory committee wants to have meetings in addition to the six provided for in the legislation, it is obligatory on the part of the board to call such meetings. In that way, no one could suggest that the advisory committee is a puppet of the minister for the Canadian Wheat Board. It would have some autonomy, some freedom of action. If circumstances arise where the advisory committee feels a meeting is warranted, the legislation should allow for that. The committee should not be limited to six meetings. Provision should be made for the payment of fees, allowances and expenses of the advisory committee meetings in those instances.

We hope that in committee the minister will tell us what he and the governor in council have in mind with regard to the drafting of regulations under amended section 10.5 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. We will be interested in knowing the ground rules for defining the borders of the electoral districts, as they are called in the legislation. What does the government have in mind with regard to the other provisions under that section? We would like some detail. Unless we have some idea of that, the minister and the governor in council could unwittingly cause things to happen that in effect detract from the need of and purpose for the Canadian Wheat Board advisory committee. I hope that in committee the minister will be willing to discuss the government's intentions with regard to regulations under the amended section 10.5 as contained in Bill C-88.
In conclusion, we support the legislation in principle. We hope the minister will consider changes of the kind I have mentioned. Further, we hope the minister will take the committee into his confidence and give us the details of what he has in mind with regard to implementing the provisions of this bill by order in council.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words with respect to this bill. Our party really has no objection to the bill. I was pleased to hear the minister say he would welcome constructive criticism on various aspects of it. I am concerned primarily with clause 4. We agree with the concept of the advisory committee. It has an important role to play in the function of the Wheat Board. However, what is most important to me is that the advisory committee be made up of actual producers. Section 10.5(3) reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations respecting the conduct of an election of members of the advisory committee and in particular, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations...
(c) prescribing the qualifications of members of the advisory committee and of actual producers for the purposes of section 10-
What has happened here is that the governor in council is given the responsibility of naming the members of the advisory committee. I can visualize a situation where we could end up with members on the committee who are not actual producers. There may not be anything wrong with that, but it is an aspect that should be looked at when the bill is in committee. If, after hearing evidence from organizations and individuals, it is the feeling of the committee that members of the advisory committee must be actual producers, the bill should be changed so that it provides that members of the advisory committee shall be producers.
We have a situation here, as we often have, where the details are not spelled out in the bill. We are governed by regulations at the whims and fancies of the governor in council. Parliament is not given the opportunity of making the decision. If it is put in the legislation by parliament, there can be no changes. As members know, regulations can be changed as often as the governor in council or the cabinet wish. I quote from a news release dated March 10, 1976, page 2, where the minister is shown as saying:
I have always thought that the lt-member advisory committee should be chosen from amongst farmers, with farmers themselves having a direct vote in their selection. It was with this thought in mind that I authorized the first election of the members of the advisory committee in 1975; the successful candidates in that election were subsequently
April 26, 1976

appointed to the committee by the governor in council as required by the act.
If it is the feeling of the minister that the members should be chosen from among the farmers, he should bring in an amendment at the committee stage to make it law. The minister has stated that he would like constructive criticism. I criticise the bill by making that suggestion. Clause 2, with regard to deferred delivery permits, is interesting. The explanatory note reads:
The purpose of this amendment is to correct errors in the present act.
If you compare the clause in the bill with the section in the act, the only change is changing the word "grain" in the original section to "wheat". I would like to know whether it is the intention that from now on deferred permits will only be granted for wheat. If you read the interpretation in the main bill, "grain" includes several types of grain. It includes wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed. By amending the section and changing it from "grain" to "wheat", unless you can stretch your imagination to say that "wheat" includes all these other grains, you end up in a situation where deferred delivery permits are only granted in the case of wheat. That will have to be looked into at the committee stage.
Clause 4 was included to remedy the situation that occurred in the 1974-75 crop year regarding malting barley. I and many other members of this House received letters from producers in the west complaining about the treatment they received with regard to their malting barley sales. I wish to quote from a typical letter that I received. It is from the town of Macrorie and is dated March 8:
Dear Mr. Neil:
I sold 1,854 bushels of barley in the 1974-75 crop year. This barley was accepted as malting barley but was graded as No. 1 feed. I have found out that the Wheat Board sold this barley at only 10 cents a bushel less than 2-CW malting barley. I would like to know why I received only 18 cents as a final payment, while producers with 2-CW barley received 99 cents a bushel. I do not think this kind of treatment is very fair. I also think that this mismanagement has to be stopped and producers in my situation should be reimbursed for the money they should have rightly received.
Instituting a separate malting pool will not help me now. I have been treated unjustly and would like to see the situation clarified. I do hope you can help me.
Mr. Speaker, my understanding, on the basis of information I have received from the minister's office and from the Wheat Board, is that in the 1974-1975 crop year there was a shortage of malting barley, the result being that maltsters purchased No. 1 feed barley from the Wheat Board to cover the shortage. Approximately one-third of the feed barley sold to the Wheat Board was sold as malting barley to the maltsters. The premium on malting barley during that period was approximately $1 a bushel.
If we look at the annual report of the Wheat Board for the crop year 1974-75, we find that No. 1 CW six-row barley realized an over-all payment of $3.26 per bushel, whereas No. 1. feed realized $2.33, approximately 90 cents a bushel less. The difference in grades 2 and 3 ranged from 90 cents to $1 a bushel. This is what individual producers are complaining about, and I can understand their feelings. I can also understand the problem faced by the Wheat Board
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) in trying to straighten out this situation, and it is for this reason we welcome the amendments contained in the bill.
The minister realized there was a problem, because he wrote to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart) with reference to a specific situation, stating:
To overcome this problem in the current year and in future crop years I introduced in parliament on March 8 an amending bill which, when approved, will enable the establishment of a separate pool for selected barley. I am enclosing for your information my press release of March 10 concerning this matter. As you are aware, changing the pooling system of the Canadian Wheat Board is not a simple matter which can be achieved overnight at the whim of myself or the board. The present system is regulated by the Canadian Wheat Board Act and in order to change that system and establish a separate pool for malting barley legislative amendments to the act must first be drafted, then considered and approved by parliament. Once the bill introduced on March 8 is approved, the returns to the board for barley which is selected and accepted by maltsters will be deposited in a separate pool. The final payment for No. 1. feed barley which was selected and accepted as malting barley will therefore fully reflect the board's selling price to the maltsters .. . The amendment will be retroactive to deliveries of malting barley in the current crop year.
So the present crop year, 1976-77, will be covered. Mr. Speaker, I have read carefully clause 4 of the bill which presumably refers to barley although I see no mention of barley in it. I know the minister will say that as far as this clause is concerned, wheat is barley; but this seems strange to me. Talk to anyone in western Canada and they will tell you that wheat is wheat and barley is barley.
