speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to enter the debate on Bill C-88 and say a few words with regard to some of the changes suggested to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. Some years ago the Canadian Wheat Board Act was renewed on a ten-year basis. In practice it came up for renewal every ten years. Two years ago the government of the day suggested that this was wrong and wanted to demonstrate its good faith in the Wheat Board by making the act permanent and doing away with the ten-year review. Since that demonstration of good faith we have seen major changes in the operation of the Wheat Board, some of which I greatly fear are to the detriment not only of the board but of the farmers in western Canada.
I always believed that the primary function of the Wheat Board was to ensure equal market opportunities and fair treatment for the farmers of western Canada. The quota system is perhaps one of the ways in which this clear and equal opportunity can be demonstrated to the farmers of western Canada; yet the authority of the Wheat Board and its ability to provide fair and equal service to the farmers of western Canada is being eroded.
The minister has come along with a feed grains proposal which allows for the open market buying of grain but which has not clearly demonstrated a pricing system for open market grain. It is a "Guess and by God" proposal which is supposed to hinge upon the initial payment plus the expected future payment. Sometimes it is relevant and sometimes it is not. It has brought about high feed grain prices for the cattle producers of western Canada, and this has caused them hardship in what might be called a very difficult period for the cattle feeding industry.
It has also caused a great deal of difficulty to the grain producers because it has tied up a great deal of storage, particularly at Vancouver. Having to keep open quota grain and Wheat Board grain in storage at Vancouver for the grain companies-really for the farmers-has caused duplication of storage of grain and has tied up bins. The Canadian Wheat Board now comes along and tells the farmers of western Canada that they are going to dock, or deduct from the final payment a certain amount of money in order to encourage the building of storage at Vancouver.
I,	personally, regret that the Wheat Board had to take this unilateral action of using the farmers' money to build storage at Vancouver. I think that the government and the grain companies could have done this on their own. I well remember the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), boasting in Calgary during the 1972 election that the government was

concentrating on overhauling Vancouver harbour and building greater storage facilities there. Well, Mr. Speaker,
I happened to look up some figures, to be found in Hansard of February 5, 1972, which indicated that the government had spent very little money in Vancouver, that in fact the amount of money spent in Vancouver between 1967 and 1972 had gone down drastically. Yet Vancouver handles something like 30 per cent of the total tonnage moving into Canada through National Harbours Board ports.
Since the minister has failed to overhaul Vancouver harbour since 1972, the Wheat Board, acting in good faith on behalf of the farmers of western Canada, have taken this task unto themselves. They have lost faith in the government and in the Minister of Transport who acts and speaks for the Wheat Board in the House of Commons. I think there is great need for further space in Vancouver because of the complicated manipulations that are involved in an open quota grain system and a Wheat Board quota system for grain. The situation will only be further complicated unless somehow or other in the regulations governing malting barley a definite grade is approved by the maltsters.
Anybody who has attempted to sell malting barley in the past knows that you can take one load of grain out of the granary and it will go malting. Yet the very next load will not go malting. What does this mean in terms of dollars and cents, Mr. Speaker? In the past year it means something like 78 cents a bushel. One farmer can sell grain as malting barley consistently. Another farmer just across the road might well believe he has harvested grain with the same low protein content, with no peel or broken kernels, yet he cannot get malting barley.
What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that I completely agree that there should be a separate pool for malting barley, but the Wheat Board at the same time should establish quite clearly a number of things. First of all, it should make quite clear that the maltsters can buy their malting barley only from the Wheat Board. If that is not made clear, the grain companies-and I fear the international grain companies because of their skill in marketing-might well be a jump ahead of the pool and in their search for customers might well use their ability to sell malting barley to the maltsters and give them a premium of some 78 or 80 cents a bushel. This would mean that the co-ops and other Canadian-owned grain companies would not be able to make sales to the maltsters.
Secondly, the Canadian Wheat Board should quite clearly lay down what in essence passes for malting barley and what does not. It should not be left to the maltsters to decide what they will accept as malting barley and what they will not accept, because I fear favouritism and that the big farmers will get the advantage over the little farmers. For example, if the maltsters want 5,000 or 10,000 bushels of grain and they can buy it all from one farmer, all from the same sample, there will be a tendency to do so. It will mean that the big farmers will get the 78 to 80 cents a bushel premium and that the small farmers will not have an equal opportunity to get the same premium.
We must always remember, Mr. Speaker, that the purpose of setting up the Canadian Wheat Board was to ensure equality and fair treatment for the prairie farmers. I have seen the erosion of this equality during the past
April 26, 1976

number of years under this minister who now speaks for the Canadian Wheat Board. While I am in complete support of a separate pool for malting barley, I see the danger of further erosion of a guarded principle that I think most farmers treasure-that of equality and fair treatment. If necessary, steps must be taken to establish a couple of clear principles-that the Wheat Board is the only body to sell to the maltsters and that the Wheat Board sets the quality or grade of malting barley, not the maltsters themselves.
While speaking on this question, I might say that I am a long-time believer in a separate pool for high protein grades and that growers of high protein wheat should get a premium. It is a well known and established fact that the farmers in northern Saskatchewan and northern Alberta are more likely to grow malting barley. This is low protein barley and has a better chance of success in the area owing to the climate in that part of the country. Barley in that area has a better chance of having no peel or broken kernels.
The very opposite is true with regard to the protein grading of wheat. It is a well known fact that farmers in southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta have a tendency to grow high protein wheat. High protein wheat is grown in what is commonly referred to as the Palliser triangle. Farmers in the Palliser triangle should get a bonus or premium for growing high protein wheat. In the past year this would have amounted to 33 cents to 35 cents per bushel. That also should be kept separate so that this premium would be paid. The net result of paying the premium on high protein wheat would be an encouragement to produce high protein wheat, and the net result of paying the premium on malting barley in a fair manner would be an encouragement to produce malting barley.
These two factors would also decrease the subsidization that now occurs in the pooling system that has been in place in the past. The premium on high protein wheat has gone into a general pool, has been divied up and has tended to maintain a higher average price for low grade wheat. The premium on malting barley has gone into a general pool with feed barley and has tended to maintain a higher average price for low or what one might call feed barley. These two facts tend to keep the price of feed grain high on the prairies. With these grains separated out, the feed grain would bring a price more comparable with what the feeding industry is prepared, willing and able to pay. I suggest this should be done.
Before this bill is passed-and I hope this is the intention of the minister-we should allow the committee to call members of the Canadian Wheat Board before it to answer a number of questions that ought to be asked. Is the open feed grain policy causing congestion at the terminals? If that is the case, as the railroads claim, we should examine that policy. That is one question I should like to ask. It has always been my belief that an open feed grains policy was designed to aid the sale of feed grains domestically rather than internationally. Why, then, is it causing congestion at the ports and terminals? This particular question should be aired and examined very thoroughly by the committee on agriculture. When this bill goes to the committee it will provide an opportunity for examination.
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
Canada Malting Co. Ltd. is one of the largest buyers of malting barley. Who owns that company? Is it true that Molson's and Labatt's have members on the board of directors of Canada Malting Co. Ltd.? Does this not bring about a conflict of interest regarding the price to be paid for malt, which in turn reflects the price to be paid for malting barley? Do the maltsters and Canada Malting seriously desire to export malt to the United States and other countries? Surely, with our ability to produce malting barley, we should be prepared to export malt to a greater extent than has been the case in the past.
Surely, it would be desirable to bring about a fair grading system for malting barley so that it could clearly be identified on each occasion and not be at the whim of the malting companies. In this way, malting barley would be clearly identifiable by farmers, grain companies and the Canadian Wheat Board. They would then know what ingredients make a sample of barley qualify for the premium.
It is a well-known fact that farmers have sent in a sample of what they felt was malting barley which has been rejected, and then sent in the same sample two weeks later and had it passed as malting barley and shipped the same carload. If we are to pay an 80-cent premium, we must have a more definitive system than the one that exists. If we do not, we will cause even more dissatisfaction over the long haul. Certainly there is a great deal of dissatisfaction today on the part of farmers who grow malting barley. They resent very much losing out on the 78-cent or 80-cent premium.
The province of Alberta grows over 50 per cent of the barley that qualifies for malting, and therefore it is the duty of Alberta members particularly to point out that our farmers want that premium. We want that premium paid to those farmers who have the capability of growing malting barley, and we want the small farmer to have an equal opportunity with the large farmer in qualifying for the premium.
Members of the Wheat Board and of the Board of Grain Commissioners should be called before the committee to clearly state that they can set up a grading principle or system which in essence will be satisfactory to the trade and, most importantly, to the producers who are to receive the premium.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) suggested that in 1974-75, 18 million bushels were bought as No. 1 feed and sold as malting barley. This is a clear case of the grain companies picking up the 80-cent premium. This is another reason the grading system has to be clearly understood by the farmers so they can prevent the grain companies from what amounts to stealing the premium. The grain company can buy up the barley as No. 1 feed, send in a sample or a mixed sample later on and qualify for the malting barley premium. It is of paramount importance that we set up a fair grading system for malting barley.
It is extremely important that the Canadian Wheat Board be given sole authority to handle malting barley under a clearly defined grading system. It is also important that the premium should be paid on high protein wheat. These two points should be made to representatives of the

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED RETROACTIVE PAYMENT TO DATE AT WHICH PERSONS ATTAINED AGE 65
speechtext:
moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider amending the Old Age Security Act to grant the Minister of National Health and Welfare the discretionary power to make retroactive payments under the Old Age Security Act to the date at which a person has attained the age of 65 years regardless of the date on which an application is received when it is shown that an applicant has failed to apply at the proper time due to sickness, justifiable ignorance, absence or for other serious and similar reasons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has come to my attention very early in my career as part of the government team that in respect of old age security there is a matter which has been of concern not only to me but, I am sure, to other members of the government and of the opposition. This concern relates to people who for some reason or other do not realize the advantages available to them in respect of the old age security pension and are not given the opportunity after one year has elapsed to have it made available to them. In such a case, obviously they lose at least one year's pension, a pension for which they have fully qualified.
I think the care of our senior citizens has become a passion for many of us. Obviously, the government has played a part in this. Representatives from countries all over the world come to Canada to study our social programs. I think we should realize that our senior citizens are the people who participated in the process of making this country great. In many ways it is because of our people who are retired that we have today a free, democratic system. Obviously, this has added to the greatness of Canada and for many of us has added to the quality of our respect not only for the old people but for the country in which we live.
The Liberal government, through its foresight and concern for not just the old people, or the senior citizens as they are now called, has over the period of its history brought in many social programs. I am afraid that on many occasions the government has neither taken nor received credit for this. At this time I think perhaps I should refer
April 26, 1976

to the credit the government should receive. Frequently in the newspapers we read of the problems governments face. Because they are governments they are criticized. However, let us look at the other side of the coin because it is obvious this has not been drawn to the attention of the people of Canada.
On many occasions we have heard of the great strides taken by the New Democratic Party, but we have not seen too much evidence of this. This is because the liberal government has won the elections. Why has the Liberal government won the elections? Is it because it has come in with promises before election time? No. It is because the Liberal government has shown the people of Canada that it listens to them and is concerned about the people of Canada both young and old. It is also because of the fact that the representations which are made to the people are acceptable to the people.
One problem in respect of this particular legislation has been the lack of retroactive payment after one year. Let us take a look at some of the reasons and some of the people who are affected by this loophole. We are very fortunate in Canada and in my riding that we have many senior citizens. The people who send congratulations to these people are amazed that some of them are 80, 90 or 100 years of age and have been married for 40, 50 or 60 years.
If I were asked why there are so many of these peop'e in my riding, I think I would say that although it is neither a riding in which there is great poverty or great prosperity, it is one in which the older people had to work long and hard for a living. They did not have the benefit of the social security programs that are available now. They had to work in order to provide a strong base for future generations. Not all of us, when we reach age 65, will be able to say we will retain 100 per cent of our faculties. Many do, but others are less fortunate. I think we must have concern for these people.
Back in the so-called old days when our society was not as mobile as it is now, the children were around the family or were in very close proximity to their parents. In many cases the parents lived in their children's homes. Now, in this mobile society, when the children grow up they have great prospects right across Canada. Many of the children look for jobs outside the proximity of their homes. When the parents reach age 65 they do not have the opportunity to go to their children and ask what they should do in respect of a certain form. They know they are entitled to the old age pension but they are not sure how to get it. Not always in all areas are offices available to such people. It would be nice to say that they could go to any town in Canada to obtain the necessary information.
We must also realize that people 65 years of age have pride. This is not a false pride. They have pride in the fact that they have gone through life supporting their children, paying their bills and attempting to have a comfortable living without depending on anyone. These people had self-sufficiency. They depended on themselves. With their pride, they ask themselves whether people would think they were becoming senile if they asked too many questions. I do not believe these people who have a fear of asking questions should be left out.
The department, of course, has done an excellent job; there is no question about that. However, it is difficult, if
Old Age Security
not impossible, for the government to follow up on every particular case. When these people find out that a one-year period has elapsed, I think they should be given an opportunity to reclaim the money which is justly theirs. The legislation was set up to take care of these people and provide them with an income. Periodically we all receive letters. I have here a letter from a lady who is a senior citizen. When she became 65 years of age, because of her pride-as I mentioned before-she did not apply for the pension. However, she was under the impression that she could draw it later, with accumulated interest. She thought the money would be held in trust and that she could withdraw it later. As we know, this is not the case.
I understand that this lady is now out helping other senior citizens. She has not only given of herself for 65 years, but is now 71 years of age is still going around helping people in her area who are not as well off monetarily or physically. She was under the impression that she could leave the money there or hold it in trust until it gained interest, after which she could take it out and spread it around to more people. I can mention other such cases; there are many across Canada.
Let us assume that a woman reaches the age of 65 first, and that her husband is five, six or ten months younger. All these years the assumption was that the husband was older. In the old days I suppose that meant something. They had lived together for 40 years, and on the wife's sixty-fifth birthday she did not claim her social insurance because she did not want it coming into the house, thus making it obvious to the husband that she was 65. There was a bond in that marriage, a bond which kept the marriage together for many years. It is a bond that the wife did not want to break because her husband felt she was the younger of the two. I am sure that on many occasions this happens. Wives in the old days had to be younger than the husband to get married. I am sure there are many Canadians in that category. Why should they be penalized for this? Why should they be penalized because of that bond and sincerity they had for perhaps 40 or 45 years?
I suggest it is time this legislation was either changed in some way or that discretionary power was given to the minister. This could be done very simply and it would show the sincerity and concern we feel, not only for the ones who apply for and receive social security but for all Canadians whom we want to enjoy the opportunities which Canada offers and which they so richly deserve.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED RETROACTIVE PAYMENT TO DATE AT WHICH PERSONS ATTAINED AGE 65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the previous speaker, has suggested that the legislation on old age security should be amended in the House.

Mr. Speaker, the motion which my colleague has presented certainly has a great deal of attraction, but I would like to examine carefully the implications of the measure he is proposing. At present an applicant has a period of two years within which it is possible for him to file an application, one year preceding his sixty-fifth birthday and one

April 26, 1976
Old Age Security
year subsequent to it during which the law permits the payment of retroactive benefits for as long as 12 months.
The motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon), is intended to permit payment of a lump sum benefit equal to at least 13 or more times the monthly amount of the benefits payable under the Old Age Security Act. Such a proposal does not really fit one of the basic objectives of the old age security program, namely, that it is an income security program for older persons designed to provide a basic current income on retirement to residents of Canada. The program is intended to provide a regular flow of income to enable those who might not have had the opportunity to set aside savings during their working careers on which to live in retirement, to meet the daily expenses of an adequate standard of living on a current basis.
The guaranteed income supplement further enforces this objective by providing additional moneys monthly for those who can demonstrate that the flow of cash receipts they have obtained within the period of the past year or less is insufficient to meet their immediate maintenance needs. I should like to say that the program is not designed to be a long-term savings plan or to provide benefit options to meet different contingencies. It is available to all eligible applicants for day to day living needs, but is not a method of capital accumulation for later withdrawal.
The requirement that an application be filed before benefits are paid is essential to the operation of the old age security program since, if potential applicants do not come forward, it would be virtually impossible to identify and locate those who are eligible in order to begin the payment of benefits. At present, an application for benefits may be filed well before eligibility for pension commences, although for administrative reasons persons are advised not to apply more than one year in advance, as I said earlier. For those who might miss the eligibility date, up to 12 full months of retroactive benefits may be paid, as I have indicated. Thus, a potential recipient has at least a full two years within which to file an application without any loss of benefits whatsoever.
It has been shown that of the Canadian population in general, 95 per cent are familiar with the old age security program. Because of their greater interest, it is not unreasonable to assume that the awareness of the program is even higher among the population approaching retirement age. My colleague, in his motion, itemized a number of circumstances which he feels would justify the increased retroactive payment of benefits. One of these is absence.
All hon. members are aware of the fact that an application for old age security benefits can only be accepted and approved from a non-resident of Canada if that person had previously resided in Canada for at least 40 years after reaching the age of 18. Therefore, in many cases an application cannot be accepted or a benefit paid to a person who is out of the country. I trust that my colleague is not suggesting that this clause should serve as a means whereby persons whose non-residence in Canada would normally disentitle them to benefits would be able to circumvent the eligibility reuqirements by applying for benefits retroactively and pleading absence.
For those persons who would be eligible to apply for benefits from abroad, the fact that they are required to

have lived in Canada for 40 years of their adult life means that they could not have left this country before the age of 58. As I mentioned earlier, they would have a full two years or more within which to remind themselves of the need to apply for the benefit and submit the application, without any loss of old age security benefits. Even our much maligned postal service would no doubt be equal to the task of delivering an application within 24 months from the very farthest corner of the globe.
Sickness is another circumstance where this greater retroactivity would apply under my colleague's suggestion. As we have heard, under the current old age security legislation a special provision is made whereby a person who cannot apply for benefits on his own behalf because of infirmity, illness or any other good reason may have someone else apply for him. Also, when a person is not sufficiently mobile to visit one of the many Old Age Security or Canada Pension Plan offices across the country, representatives of these offices will make home visits-a service which few ill persons can expect even from their doctors these days.
Justifiable ignorance is another reason which is accepted in awarding larger retroactive benefits. "Ignorance" is a rather open-ended word. Ignorance of what? Are we speaking about ignorance of the program? If so, let us look at that question. As I said earlier, 95 per cent of the full age range of the population know about the old age security program. As personal interest in such things grows with the proximity of potential benefits, the older age groups who are thinking of retirement-let us say from 55 years and up, an age group about which I am particularly sensitive-are doubtless even more aware of the program.
Of the population aged 65 and over, more than 98 per cent are receiving old age security benefits. Of the remainder, less than 2 per cent who are not receiving the benefits-a goodly number, approaching 1.5 per cent-would not be eligible for the benefits because they do not meet the residence requirements. Others who are not receiving the benefit at one point in time, although eligible, will apply and begin to receive it within a year, and so are covered by the existing retroactivity provision.
Once we eliminate all these groups, we are left with very few potential cases. Who are the people in this group? Their most important characteristic which we should consider is their financial position. If someone over 65 is in financial need and seeks assistance from virtually any source in this country, he or she will be made aware, if they are not already, of the old age security benefits available to them. Social assistance agencies, private benefit plans, financial counsellors, retirement groups and friends all know of the program and would refer them to the old age security program. One quarter of the people over 65 who do not receive old age security do receive some other form of government transfer payment and therefore are doubtless aware of the old age security program.
Of course, in some cases pride enters into the question. My hon. friend discussed pride-pride upon which, presumably, a marriage survived over a long period of time. I understand the circumstances and I find them a little unusual. However, it is not unusual for a retired person to
April 26, 1976

refuse government income even though he or she is in need. This position can, and does, apply to old age security as much as to other public benefits. Where persons of their own free will choose not to apply for OAS benefits, as they are entitled to do, I question whether the government can or should interfere with that choice. Again, where it can be shown medically that such a choice is the result of physical or mental deterioration, some other person may apply for the benefit of behalf of the beneficiary. Finally, there are those in our society who are in the happy position of not needing OAS benefits. For these people the limit on retroactivity is not a financial hardship.
I wish to reiterate that OAS benefits are designed to provide current income to meet day to day needs. Although, as a result of various circumstances, a person may meet these needs by some other means for an extended period of time, this should not serve to transform the basic purpose of the program to that of a means of capital accumulation.
There is another type of ignorance to which we might refer. That is personal ignorance of one's own age. In a limited number of cases when people come forward to apply for OAS benefits and are asked to provide proof of age, they discover that they are older, sometimes by several years, than they had always thought themselves to be. With more accurate records, and so on, this situation will become less and less common. However, for those in this situation now the late determination of their true age means the loss of OAS benefits. Of course, this discovery will affect more than just OAS, and the interaction of a large retroactive OAS payment with other affected benefits or legislation must be considered. Payments under the Canada assistance plan, war veterans' allowances and some private pension plans are fully or partially offset by OAS benefits. A long-term retroactive payment of OAS benefits would retroactively affect the recipient's status under such programs or plans. In addition, there are the possible income tax effects of the receipt of a large cash benefit payment in any one year.
Finally, the hon. member's motion states that where an acceptable reason for late application is presented, the OAS benefit is to be paid retroactively to the date at which the person attained age 65 in all cases. I want to talk about this. Such a provision, if interpreted in the manner in which I think it could be interpreted, would introduce a far greater and more serious inequality than that which the motion purports to remedy.
Let us consider one or two possible hypothetical cases. The proposal might entitle a person to a retroactive benefit for the full period from age 65, even though had he or she applied for that benefit at age 65, he or she would not have been eligible for the payment at that time. This would occur when the applicant had ten years continuous residence at, say, age 68 and applied then for a retroactive benefit on the ground of justifiable ignorance. However, at age 65, with only seven years of residence, that same person would not have qualified for OAS.
Another example to which I referred briefly earlier is the applicant who is resident in Canada at age 68 when the application is made for the retroactive benefit, but at age 65 was living abroad and did not have long enough Canadian residence to qualify for receipt of OAS benefits abroad
Old Age Security
at that time. I must concede that these are hypothetical cases, and the hon. member who proposed the motion might well agree that it would be possible to make amendments in drafting the legislation in such a way as to make sure that the clear intent of parliament when the legislation was introduced would not be thwarted.
I suggest that there is no major inequity in the present situation. I am suggesting to hon. members that they must look at the basic objective of the program, and that is to provide a decent standard of living, so far as possible, on a current basis. The purpose of the program is not to provide a savings program, not to accumulate assets and not to accumulate credits. For these reasons, I suggest that this House might want to think fairly carefully before extending the period of retroactivity under the legislation.

speechtext:
Yes, and others apply automatically. Or there could be peculiar circumstances which inhibit an application.
The hon. member suggests in his motion that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) should be given discretionary power:
... to make retroactive payments under the Old Age Security Act to the date at which a person has attained the age of 65 years regardless of the date on which an application is received when it is shown that an applicant has failed to apply at the proper time due to sickness, justifiable ignorance, absence or for other serious and similar reasons.
Old age security gives a monthly income to the retired. The phrase in the motion "regardless of the date on which an application is received" troubles me. You see, Mr. Speaker, if we adopt this part of the motion we shall open the door for all sorts of abuse. What if a person waited five or six years before applying? He would be entitled to a lump sum payment. I do not think the original act intended that. I respect the hon. member's motives; they are grand. But there is a fault here.
The motion speaks of an applicant who fails to apply at the proper time due to sickness. Well, someone else can apply on the applicants' behalf. There are such procedures. Surely uncles, aunts, brothers, sisters, even parents, of the sick can forward applications. There is entitlement to old age security if the proper application is made.
The motion then uses the word, "that an applicant has failed to apply-due to-justifiable ignorance." It is an interesting phrase, but I don't know what it means. Does it mean ignorance of the law, ignorance of this motion, or ignorance of rights? And what is "justifiable" ignorance? That is open to interpretation in court, and we all know what happens in court when lawyers argue.
The concluding words of the motion are, "-absence or for other serious and similar reasons." Absence is a tricky word. Does it apply to residency? If it does, it could frustrate the legitimate intention of the law having to do with residency periods. And the last few words, "-or for other serious and similar reasons" are merely a catch-all phrase defying definition. I say all this while conceding the hon. member's good intentions.
All this talk of senior citizens reminds me of the minister's bill which was to provide spouses' allowances. There was a great hue and cry all over this country when the bill was first introduced. Members of parliament heard from widows, widowers, single people and divorced people, those who had not reached 65 and were not married legally, and those who were 65 or over but were not able to get the allowance. After all, the idea of the supplement was to make life more tolerable. I am still getting letters about the spouses' allowance. People take a dim view of it. It seems to me that under the minister's proposal-and I say this with sincerity-people living in sin could be entitled to spouses' allowance, whereas 60-year old widows, widowers, single people and divorced people would be put out the pasture, so to speak.
The hon. member's proposal involves money; I do not know how much. He mentioned 5 per cent of the people being affected by it. Apparently 5 per cent of our people,

for some reason, do not apply for benefits. I wish the hon. member had told the House how much money his proposal would cost. These are days of restraint. Even so I recognize that, because inflation has eroded the value of our dollar, some people are in dire need of financial assistance. We ought to be concerned about them.
In my opinion the present law allows those who cannot themselves apply, or have failed to apply, one year's retroactive benefits. Really that is a lump sum payment. The government provided for a sort of trust fund and took cognizance of the kind of situation about which the hon. member is concerned. No matter when you apply, you cannot get more than one year's benefits.
I do not want to talk the motion out. The hon. member brought the motion before the House for the edification of members and their constituents. This debate has shown that we are always thinking and want to improve the lot of those who did so much to develop this country. Even so, I suggest that the number of people the motion would affect is not great.
In conclusion I say that it is our responsibility as members of parliament to advise constituents, especially people falling within the purview of the motion, of government programs set up for their benefit. As I said earlier, the government should vote money every year to advertise these programs. I do not know what it would cost, but it would be a dollar well spent if there were an advertisement, even once a year, advising people of programs such as this.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon) is learning this afternoon what it is like to be a member of the opposition. He got hold of a good idea, he brought it before the House, he was hopeful it would be received favourably but has found that it is being jumped on by his friends and opponents and that in due course, it will be talked out.
If the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton had proposed a wide open provision that would enable persons to defer taking old age security for five or ten years and then pick up a nest egg with interest and so on, that proposal might have deserved the kind of criticism that was given by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) and in part by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. However, I want to emphasize, in supporting the hon. member's idea, that he is not asking for a wide open provision. He is simply asking that in certain special cases there be more discretionary power than there is at the present time. The act now provides, and it is spelled out in the regulations under the act, that a regional director can go back at least a year. All that the hon. member is proposing is that it be possible to go back further than that in special cases.
It is possible to criticize some of the reasons the hon. member has put forward. However, all he has placed before us is a resolution. This is not the language to be put in a bill. I am sure he would agree that the language in a bill could be more restrictive.
Both of the last speakers have suggested that not very many persons are affected by this situation. I can testify to
April 26, 1976

that as well. I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West that Canadians from 55 up pretty well know what the provisions are with respect to old age security and are ready to apply when the time comes. However, I remind the House that not many months ago the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) brought up a case of one person, a veteran, who had stayed in the United Kingdom for some years after the war. He failed to meet the precise qualifications even though he was a Canadian in all other respects. It was finally agreed by the government that, even if there were only a few cases, here was an injustice that should be corrected. That injustice has been corrected, or at least is in the process of being corrected.
I receive a great deal of correspondence about pension matters, but I have had only two persons write to me about this matter because if affects them. However, they are extremely grateful that an injustice has been corrected. That is one of the things that is great about parliament; if there is an injustice, even if it affects only a very few persons, it deserves to be corrected.
I quite agree with those who say we should not go hogwild in this. However, I believe there is room for a greater element of discretion where there is a clear, justifiable reason for a person failing to apply for old age security within the year that is now stipulated in the legislation.
Even though the hon. member many suffer the fate of other private members and see his motion talked out at six o'clock, I hope that his having raised the matter for discussion will result in its being considered in the department. If he has cases that are specific, such as those to which he referred, he would be well advised to present them to the department. Others of us should do the same so that an injustice, even to a half dozen individuals, does not remain in our statutes.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I give my general support to the intent of motion presented by the hon. member. I will refrain from participating in any talking out process. In fact all I will say before I sit down is that I am glad the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) raised an issue which most of us think is of very great importance right now. I refer to the discrimination being experienced and felt by thousands of Canadians who are spinsters, widows, bachelors, and widowers in the age bracket between 60 and 65.
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) brought in Bill C-62 in June, 1975, he stood in this House and said that what he was trying to do was to solve the problem of two persons living on one pension. That is his plausible excuse for this arrangement that pays a pension, on a means test basis, between 60 and 65 to a person who is married and living with a spouse over 65, but not to a person in the same age bracket who is alone. Indeed the spinster, widow, bachelor or widower in this country who is between 60 and 65 cannot understand why a pension is available to a woman of the same age who has a husband over 65, but is not available to the woman who is a widow or who is not married. That is an issue that should be corrected in this very session of parliament.
I realize this is beyond the confines of the motion before us, but each member who has had the floor so far has gone beyond those confines for a moment. I shall settle for what
Old Age Security
I have said. Although there are many things that need to be done in the pension field, one fact above all others that is annoying thousands of Canadians today is this discrimination of the spouses' allowance in that it discriminates against single persons between the ages of 60 and 65. I hope that will soon be corrected.
I sit down simply saying again that despite the rough ride the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton has had, I hope that his bringing this issue before the House will result in the matter being considered, at least in the department.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (No. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-88, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (No. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act are always the subject of great interest to western farmers. The Canadian Wheat Board is a very unique institution about which Canadians should know much more. Under the Canadian Wheat Board Act of 1935 we give the power to this independent board to buy the grains of western Canada, and we give the power to this independent board to sell the grains of western Canada, so that in one sense parliament, by drawing power from the provincial governments, has delegated monopoly power to the board to sell the goods of a very large productive area of Canada, the grain growing area of the western provinces, including parts, of B.C. and Ontario.
This organization or institution is unique, as I say. Even though it has all the powers that our so-called socialist would say he stands for, of delegating to a board complete monopoly over the buying and selling of a farmer's product, actually it is not a selling board and it is not a monopoly in the real sense of the word. What the board does that makes it unique is that in turn it delegates its power to be the sole agent that buys the grain of the farmers to private enterprise. It delegates its power to the grain companies such as the great co-operatives, the Alberta Pool, the Saskatchewan Pool, the Manitoba Pool, and to
April 26, 1976

the UGG. These are supposed to be the greatest co-operatives in the world in terms of the volume of business that they do.
At the same time it delegates the power to any group of people who have enough money and responsibility to go to the Wheat Board and buy the grain from the farmers as the board's agent, so that any group of people who can collect the money have the right, under the management of the Canadian Wheat Board, to become the agent of the board and, in effect, provide competition among the buyers or agents of the board in the buying of grain from the farmers.
That is one side of the equation. When the board transfers the grain from the farmer through its agent, these private companies, it then turns the power to sell-which is a monopoly-over to a series of agents, so that any group of people, Canadian or foreign, who can prove to the Wheat Board they have the financial responsibility can become agents of the Canadian Wheat Board and sell all over the world.
I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that not only do many people across Canada not understand how the Canadian Wheat Board operates but many people in the west are uncertain too. We do not get too many opportunities to discuss the Canadian Wheat Board and the amendments made from time to time to the act.
This unique institution has worked exceptionally well. It has attempted to give to the farmers a fair price averaged over the year. The technique it uses is to give an initial payment, and when the grain is sold to give an interim or final payment, and this is averaged grade by grade.
To put the matter into perspective, I do not think there is any question but that 85 to 90 per cent of the farmers have been reasonably satisfied with the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board over the last 40 years. However, that does not mean that there has been complete satisfaction; doubts do arise from time to time.
One of the amendments in Bill C-88 which is before us is to set down the terms for electing an advisory board based on districts in the grain growing area. This is an amendment that I am positive every political party in western Canada supports. We have no choice but to congratulate the government on putting this proposal into law, and I am going to give the House some reasons why those congratulations are worth-while and necessary.
There always has been an advisory board. Under the original act power was given to the minister to appoint members to an advisory board, and as a general rule the minister picked the heads of the big grain organizations as members of the board to advise the Wheat Board. When I was minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board I added an additional person, a representative of the National Farmers' Union. Why, then, do I say that an elected advisory board is better? The reasons are very simple.
When you began to watch, observe, and assess what the old advisory board was contributing to the actions of the Wheat Board you got the strong impression that the advisory board you had appointed yourself, made up of the heads of the big grain companies, was in fact very friendly
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) and cosy with members of the Canadian Wheat Board. They were there representing not only their farmers and their organizations, they were representing the businesses they managed, and as managers they were very anxious to have this system work smoothly and efficiently. You rarely got criticism from these people about the actions of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Remember what I said earlier-the Canadian Wheat board selected these companies as its agents. Therefore it was a meeting really of top management, the Canadian Wheat Board and the advisory board which was in effect the agent of the Canadian Wheat Board. It was naturally a cosy relationship.
The great grain companies are very large and they make good returns. Their first responsibility to their rank and file is to maintain the profit margin they have obtained through the handling of grain. I got the impression, as the minister watching their activities, that this was not really the type of advice I thought the farmers deserved when they had to rely on the Canadian Wheat Board. That is the reason why I added the farm unions, hoping they would represent these farmers in a better way, not having a vested interest and not having a great army of country or seaboard terminals to manage. Even this was not too strong a representation for the simple reason that we soon found out the National Farmers' Union rarely disagreed with the wheat pools.
Therefore I say with all sincerity to the minister that by putting this board in as an elected board, giving the farmers directly a chance to elect their representatives to advise the Wheat Board, he is going to get a little more independent type of advice as well as criticism of the Canadian Wheat Board. Even if the Wheat Board were made up of the most perfect people in the world it could not be anything more than human, and it makes mistakes, but it is nice to know there are at least ten or 11 independent elected people representing their electors, watching what is going on and giving advice.
With these advisory meetings as laid down in the amendments I hope this will result in more cogent criticism of the Canadian Wheat Board. This will make it even better than it has been. Just as an example let me refer to a report of one of the independent members who got himself elected. He comes from the province of Alberta and he submitted a report of which I have a copy here. Just listen to his language, and remember that this is a report of an elected representative on the advisory board which we are now legalizing by this legislation. He says in this report:
Did you know: that grade and dockage must be agreed upon by both the elevator agent and the farmer?
That is a routine question. He goes on to state:
A "subject to grade" storage ticket ensures that a government inspector will grade this grain; or you can have a sample government inspected at the government inland terminals. If to your advantage, haul it there, consign it to the elevator company of your choice and receive the $ benefit of official grade and dockage.
Then he says:
(For example, a government inspected sample of your barley may grade 2 CW Barley instead of 1 Feed Barley, to your advantage of 91 cents a bushel.)
I stop there, but that is the type of advice he is giving. This type of thing has been known all along, but not too

April 26, 1976
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
often have we found people who are advising the farmers and being so frank with them. In fact this advisory member of the board is telling the farmers in his area to make sure they shop around and get the best price from the grain companies.
I was struck by this because I am sure one of the reasons why we have this amendment before us is that there has been a squabble over barley this last year. This is dealt with in clause 4 of the bill. Under this amendment it will be possible for the Wheat Board to set up a malting barley pool. No member has to be told that barley is of several grades. In addition to being of several grades, some of it is selected in a very mysterious manner and called malting. Very few people, if any, are able to tell us or the farmers exactly what is a malting grade of barley. You can haul one load in from your granary and the elevator man will look at it and say it is malting. You can then bring in another load from the same granary and he might look at it and say it is No. 1 feed. The farmers have been unable for years to find out what it is that makes some barley malting and some feed grain, but the price is different. This year it was some 91 cents different.
As the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) was saying before the dinner recess, the key to making this part of the bill work is strict definition of grades. With the knowledge and experience of the elevator agents I think they require a type of description which has never been given before. Some farmers, who for years have been getting malting, will suddenly not get malting but will get No. 1 feed. This year with that 91-cent a bushel spread this represented a very serious loss. My point here is that I think the hon. member for Crowfoot was not gilding the lily when he used the word "stealing".
The grain act makes it very plain that every time a farmer hauls grain to an elevator the law of Canada requires that the farmer be paid for what he delivers. For that reason it is very necessary to have a clear definition of the difference between the various grades we have been using for years. If a farmer does not like the grade given by an elevator agent he can appeal to a government inspector and to the Board of Grain Commissioners. Theirs is the final decision. This system has worked very well over the years. It is very important that the law be carried out, and that each farmer is paid for what he delivers.
No one has told me as yet the full story of what happened last year. Apparently the farmers took in their barley. Many of them got feed grades, and no one knows why. Later on it was discovered there was not enough malting barley on hand, so they took the barley which had been graded No. 1 feed, which gets a lower price, and arbitrarily raised it to malting, and then made the maltsters pay another 91 cents a bushel for that malting barley. Somewhere along the line the farmers were done out of the full 91 cents difference for malting barley.
The hon. member for Crowfoot suggested that the difference went into the accounts of the grain companies. I have heard another story, namely, that it was the Wheat Board that mixed the grain at the terminals up to a malting barley grain which the maltsters accepted. The board took this excess money for this barley that was raised up in grade and distributed the extra money equally in respect of all No. 1 feed deliveries. Some got 18 cents extra and

some got 91 cents extra, and that is what the issue is all about.
I understand from reading the press that a number of farmers have grouped together in Alberta and are suing the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain companies for many millions of dollars because they claim they got No. 1 feed grade for their barley and found out that this was later graded malting barley, yet they only got a final 18 cents a bushel extra payment. In effect they are accusing the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain companies of stealing their grain and are asking for recompense in a class action. I suspect that is the reason for this sudden amendment. This is being made retroactive so that it can be legitimately pooled this year and so that there will be some way to know that the farmer receives the amount of money he should receive rather than having it given to the grain companies or having it spread over all the feed grades.
I say that even though the Canadian Wheat Board has a long record of successful activity that satisfies the great bulk of the farmers, every so often something goes wrong. When it comes to not paying the farmer for the grade of grain as delivered to the elevator and when he is not given the exact price for the exact grade, it is in effect stealing from that farmer and is in breach of the Grain Act.
This brings up the third point I want to make. Twice this afternoon the necessity of protein grading has been mentioned. I think the minister has been very delinquent in not taking the opportunity to get amendments into the act and in not having used this opportunity to make it mandatory that the grain companies provide protein grading at the elevators. Going back 20 years, the argument was that it was impossible for the Board of Grain Commissioners and for the Canadian Wheat Board to grade at the elevators. It was argued that the elevator men were not smart enough to carry out the protein grading technique. That was always a fallacy. So long as the farmers were paid on the basis of the number of pounds brought to the elevator and on the basis of the colour, there was no breach of the law. Now that we are not selling grain on the basis of pounds and colour but on the basis of protein content it is a different story.
Today we are selling at the coasts to overseas buyers wheat graded on an average of 13.5 or 12.5 per cent protein. That is what we are paid for. Our customers demand a guaranteed percentage of protein in the wheat they buy. They are buying protein and not wheat. Therefore under the Grain Act if you sell grain on the basis of protein content you must pay the individual farmer in respect of what he delivered to the elevator on the basis of what it is sold for, and if it is sold on the basis of protein content he should be paid at that rate. If this is not the case then there will be a breach of the Grain Act because this will represent stealing from the individual farmer. Therefore the minister, who knows all this, should have attempted to put into this legislation a clear mandatory direction that grain be graded on a protein content basis so that each farmer would know the amount of protein he delivered. If the grain were mixed after that, that would be fair enough. But the farmer should be paid on the basis of percentage of protein he delivered.
April 26, 1976

I say very bluntly to the minister that I suspect that so long as we continue buying from the farmer on the basis of the existing grading at the elevator, and turn around and sell his grain on a different basis of protein grade, the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain companies are in breach of the Grain Act and are subject to class actions for damages by the farmers when they get mad enough and find out about it.
The minister should have been on top of this. He should have forced the grain companies to modernize their systems and put in this type of grading. I think that is what we should have been discussing here tonight because I believe it is even more important than just the barley malting pool. The principle in both cases is identical.
The pool system is being amended to provide a malting pool so that the farmers will be paid for what they deliver. Why should the farmers not be paid for what they deliver on the basis of the protein content of the wheat, which is nine or ten times more important relatively than the barley problem?
I suggest that the royal commission which is now holding hearings in the west on transportation and grain handling should make a very strong recommendation that the Canadian Wheat Board be asked to have the Canadian Wheat Board Act amended to make it mandatory that the Board and its agents, the grain companies, pay the farmers for what they deliver to the elevator on the basis of the protein grade of the delivered wheat.
I am very annoyed that after all these years, when we have an opportunity to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, we do not get at this basic weakness which has existed ever since Canada began to sell on the basis of protein grade from the elevators. I realize this means that the elevator companies will have to be modernized so that they can not only buy the grain and dry the grain but also grade it on a protein basis.
Once again may I say I think this royal commission should very strongly recommend to the government that the elevator companies be asked, as the royal commission has asked the railway companies, to bring in a rational plan for elevators all through the prairies instead of having this 30-year old long drawn out struggle to avoid giving up older elevators in place of the modern ones we should have had 30 years ago. Now that the elevator companies are exposed I think they should be asked by the royal commission, just as the railways were asked, to bring in a rational plan to modernize elevators so that we are not overwhelmed by irrational building by the various companies. I hope the royal commission will see that as a good recommendation to make. Naturally I would have liked the government to have heeded the pressure of public demand and common sense and to have done it in this legislation.
The next point I wish to make is one that does not require an amendment. There is an interesting clause in section 25(2) of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I will read this section because it deals with farm storage:
The Board shall,-
I think this is understood by the minister.
-if directed by regulation, pay to each producer at the time of delivery of wheat to the Board, in addition to any other payment authorized by
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
this section, a sum per bushel on account of storage of the said wheat on the producer's farm,...
If we are to have a rational grain storage system both at the sea coast terminals and at the country terminals, into that storage system must be built, if we are to have a rational plan, some provision for farm storage. I bring this up particularly in respect of the branch lines.
There has been an ongoing difference of opinion between the farmers and the railroads on these branch lines where the steel is not too good and where the roadbed has not been maintained during the last 20 or 30 years. These branch lines do not operate in the winter months. In some cases where the lines have been built up it is relatively easy for the railway to keep them open and service them in the winter, but there are many hundreds of miles of branch lines where it will be many years, and require the expenditure of many millions of dollars, before they are raised high enough and will be of heavy enough steel to warrant their being kept open during the winter season when the snow has drifted across the tracks.
If the railways could save money by not having to operate trains on those branch lines which only require one train a week, for example, if those trains were stopped for the winter-as most of them are now anyway-so the railways would not have to expend money to snowplough the tracks,-if the railways were given instructions from the Canadian Transport Commission to let these lines lie idle during the winter months, then the farmers along those lines would be quite satisfied if they had the opportunity to get paid for the grain stored on their farms during the periods of non-delivery. They would be glad to store this grain at half the rate that the grain companies demand.
It is an injustice to the farmer who cannot get his grain into the elevators in the fall, and who cannot transport it in the winter because of lack of movement of trains, that he cannot take advantage of the provision in the act which allows the Canadian Wheat Board to pay for the storage of his grain on his own farm until the spring. If he kept his grain on his farm, and assuming it did not interfere with the Wheat Board deliveries to market, he could be compensated at 5 cents a month or 3 cents for six months, and he would be quite satisfied that justice had been done.
I would have liked to have heard some mention made by the minister that he was aware of the fact that this should have been part of the over-all rationalization of the handling of grain on the western farms which would not force the railways to go to extra expense if they did not have to, and at the same time which would allow grain to be held back from lines which would not have to be kept open in the winter. It would be fair both to the grain companies and the farmers along the lines if they got paid for their storage as were farmers along other lines who got their grain into the elevators or could get it to market. I put this suggestion forward knowing that it does not require an amendment to the act because the act allows it now. This requires a decision of the minister and of the Canadian Wheat Board, and I would like to see them think about it and do something about it rather than being told by the

April 26, 1976
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) royal commission, when it reports in a year or so, that this should have been done.
In summary, what I have tried to do tonight is to put in perspective the work of the Canadian Wheat Board in serving the western farmer as equitably and fairly as it can, to point out that the minister should be congratulated for having made the advisory committee an elected body which we hope can give good advice to the Wheat Board, and to give the minister a little bit of a poke to amend the act insofar as the barley malting pool is concerned. This pool is necessary to get around the difficulty which arose last year, not only because it arose once but because it was so serious last year that we had to amend the act. I should like to suggest very strongly that the minister made a great error in not making protein grading mandatory. I think this should be part of a comprehensive, rational system. I think this amendment would meet with the approval of most members from western Canada, but I could not resist the opportunity to put forward a few suggestions that would have made it much better.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (No. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this bill. First of all I should like to speak on the portion dealing with the advisory committee. I think I can accept what the minister has done, although I will say that I had hoped the advisory committee would keep the Wheat Board closer to the producers and closer to the principle on the basis of which the Board was established. We have to remember that in the last six or seven years the political process had a great deal of influence on what has gone on in Wheat Board circles.
As I understand it, the Wheat Board was given the specified duty of getting for the farmers the best price that their product could bring, whether it was selling abroad or in Canada. It is quite easy to sell abroad at a good price, but it is not always so easy to sell the product well in Canada particularly when it comes to feed grains and products consumed in other parts of Canada. For instance, if feed barley is sold by the western farmer, should he receive all the money he can get on the world market or should he in the national interest accept a lesser price in order to give the feeder in eastern Canada an advantage or to eliminate excess price?
It is important that the Wheat Board be as close to the farmers as possible, and that the advisory committee to be elected by the farmers act as a watch dog on what the Wheat Board is doing. It should be noted that the Wheat Board will function best if the political input from Ottawa is kept down to the minimum.
I should like to comment on the problem of barley which this bill seeks to rectify. It has come about because the producers of No. 1 feed barley this year are now seeing red. A good many of them have lost more than $2,000 a car lot because their earnings were lumped into the same pool as funds from lower priced feed barley.
Indications that a separate pool for selected and accepted barley will be instituted this year are not going down too well with producers who lost heavily in the past year. As some producers have said:
It has never been this bad. It's the same as if someone puts their hand in your pocket and takes $2,000.

At this point we're unwilling to accept this kind of legislation. We feel there is mismanagement to the point where the government should rectify their errors.
It has all come about because of the shortage of malting barley and the fact that some feed barley was put in but the grower of better grade barley did not receive his proper return.
I have received a letter from a constituent, who made what I thought was a very good comment, in which he stated that he hoped that any proposed legislation and change would be retroactive to the 1974-75 crop year at least because this was the crop year when any significant difference in the pricing of the two types of barley took place. He writes:
Feed barley producers who have had their final payments increased by selected barley producers in 1974-75 should have no objection to have their final payments reduced by a like amount in 1975-76 to correct a situation that should never have been allowed to exist in the first place.
He suggests that the only known way to correct a wrong is by making it right. He goes on to say that it is not just luck that a barley sample is selected for malting. Malting barley requires any number of conditions which do not necessarily apply to feed barley. First, a variety must be grown which is acceptable to maltsters, and most barley varieties have disadvantages. They are usually lower yielding than feed varieties. They generally require earlier seeding to mature. They are more intensive and need more expensive weed control. They need proper timing of swathing to avoid damage by frost or shrinkage. Harvesting is a problem, and more care must be taken. Cleaning and marketing are more variable.
I think the minister in charge of the Wheat Board should consider what he could do for barley producers who have found themselves caught out this year. It is certainly true that many farmers do try to raise malting barley. They give it extra attention, but very often they do not succeed because of conditions beyond their control. When they do have the good luck and the good fortune to have a carload of malting barley, they should receive benefit from their work.
There is one other clause in the bill which interests me. It is clause 5 at page 8 of the bill. The explanation given of this clause is to correct an anomaly in the act since the act does not provide for an initial payment in respect of rye, flaxseed, and rapeseed. I should like to hear an explanation of the purpose of this clause from the minister because it is my understanding with regard to rye, flaxseed, and rape-seed on the open market that there would be no necessity to have an initial payment unless it was decided to put these under the Wheat Board. However, I think it is important that before any of these grains be put under the Wheat Board the views of the majority of producers be ascertained in the usual manner.
Because there is not usually very much opportunity to discuss the problems of the wheat grower, I should like to speak about a problem which is common to the northern part of the prairies, particularly my area, which is a parkland area. All wheat now grown in the parkland area, which I understand this year is approximately 100 million bushels, is grown in the area stretching from the Peace River country through northern Alberta, northern Sas-
April 26, 1976

katchewan and on into Manitoba. All of it is pretty well graded No. 3 Red this year. The next grade below No. 3 Red is No. 3 Utility wheat, or what is commonly known as feed wheat.
The price differential between No. 3 Red and No. 3 Utility is anywhere from 40 cents a bushel to 60 cents a bushel. This seems to have come about because of the change in the grading system, and it is causing a great deal of consternation and reassessment about what farmers should grow in my area. We in the parkland area have always accepted that we grow lower protein wheat, but generally speaking we grow more bushels, and by and large there has always been a market around the world for the parkland wheat even if it has not commanded the same high price as southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta wheat.
The recent changes in the grading system seem to have made No. 3 Red wheat a relatively unwanted variety,in the grain trade. The changeover from the grading system meant, presumably, that No. 1 and No. 2 were to go into the new No. 1 Red; No. 3 and No. 4 were to go into No. 2 Red; No. 5 and a bit of No. 6 were to go into No. 3; and the balance of No. 6 and feed wheat were to go into the new grade 3 utility. However, while the drawings and the propaganda put out by the Board of Grain Commissioners have these all neatly circled, in practice I have found that the government grading system as well as that of elevator agents-and they are not to blame-is that they are putting pretty well all wheat in the parkland area in No. 3 Red. In other words, they are really grading protein by areas.
I had occasion to take a sample of wheat to two individual elevator buyers. I asked them what this would grade under the old system, and they said it was at least a poor No. 3 or a good No. 4. This should have put it into the grade 2 Red, but in effect it did not because the Board of Grain Commissioners people graded all this No. 3 Red, which is considerably below what it would have graded under the old grading system.
What is the effect of this? The effect has been that No. 3 Red wheat has had a hard job this year finding a market around the world. Many farmers in my constituency have delivered no wheat this year because there was no room. One country point only had ten cars in the last four months, none of which was No. 3 Red wheat. Even No. 3 Utility wheat is moving faster than No. 3 Red. Furthermore, elevator agents and farmers point out that the difference between No. 3 Red and No. 3 Utility was 60 cents a bushel last year, 40 cents a bushel this year, and that the difference between grading No. 3 Red and No. 3 Utility in many cases is not easy.
These changes are having a very adverse effect on the grading of wheat on many millions of acres. I should like to know why this is. Is there some collusion, so to speak, between the Wheat Board, the Board of Grain Commissioners and grain handling companies? It will obviously be easy for the Wheat Board to sell grades 1 and 2 around the world. The percentage of high grade wheat moving in international circles has remained fairly high, at 26 per cent or 27 per cent. It has been fairly consistent over the last number of years.
Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2)
But what about No. 3 Red? That is a harder thing to sell, whereas previously it was easily sold, particularly this past year. Is the Wheat Board always making an effort to sell No. 3 Red wheat? A good deal of the wheat is being pushed down into No. 3 Utility and into feed grain, and I suspect that the Wheat Board does not find this all that bad because it is relieved of attempting to dispose of a sizeable portion of the No. 3 Red crop around the world. I think this is unfortunate.
I think we are doing ourselves out of a market, and as the amount of grain involved is one hundred million bushels at $4 or $5 a bushel, that represents half a billion dollars. If this is lost, our farmers and our economy are certainly much worse off. If grain is not going to be graded any higher than No. 3 Red and if it will not be easily sold, there may be a shift in farming practices. I suggest that in the new grading system there should be another grade between No. 3 Red and feed wheat.
Of course, having the new system has been advantageous to grain handling companies because it has reduced their binning requirements necessary to carry out more grades. Grading is not uniform. I have known elevator agents say, "If you were in southern Saskatchewan I could grade this grain as No. 1; but here we must grade it as No. 3." That shows that the grading system is hazy in operation and not serving the farmers. I hope the minister and the grain commissioners will look at the matter and correct it. Possibly the solution lies in introducing another grade which could be equivalent to Nos. 5 and 6 under the old grading system. This, I think, would best serve the farming community, particularly the farming community of western Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring two or three matters to the attention of hon. members, particularly those interested in the production and movement of grain. I suggest that all hon. members ought to be vitally interested in what is happening to prairie grain on world markets, as grain sales vitally affect our country's well-being. We sell about $3 billion worth of grain on world markets. These grain sales improve our balance of trade, something we should not forget.
I was concerned, on returning to this House, to discover that the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, who is also the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang)-
