speechtext:
-and acting House leader could not answer our questions during the question period. He said he did not know the answers. Obviously the reason is that he has not been in Ottawa, keeping in touch with events; he has been in western Canada, traipsing around in the Jetstar and trying to sell his stabilization bill to producers. The minister reminds me of Nero who fiddled while Rome burned. He was fiddling around in western Canada, trying to sell a program not too acceptable to western grain producers. By accepting our advice he could have designed a workable program. He would not have needed to spend several weeks out west trying to sell his program to producers. When he appeared in Red Deer, two known Liber-

Canadian Wheat Board Act (No. 2) als clapped their hands-not at what he said, but perhaps because he is such a good looking fellow.
We question certain aspects of this bill and will consider them further, in detail when the bill is in committee. In some ways the faults of this bill are similar to the faults of the grain stabilization bill. As was pointed out at the meeting in Red Deer, the grain stabilization bill is dictatorial, as is this bill. After the stabilization program has been in place three years, the producer cannot opt out. He is locked in. Orders in council can raise or lower tariffs, but it is dangerous to introduce a program from which the producer cannot opt out. The same is true of the bill we are considering.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (No. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That's nonsense. You can't opt out of the Canada Pension Plan.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD ACT (No. 2) MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTION OF MEMBERS OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, but the government is assuming too much control over the administrative aspects of the bill. I know that on second reading we are not supposed to speak in detail on the clauses of the bill. Nevertheless, allow me to read part of proposed section 10.5(3) wherein it says:
The Governor in Council may make regulations respecting the conduct of an election of members of the Advisory Committee and in particular, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations . ..
The following subparagraphs specify that there shall be regulations prescribing the qualifications of members of the advisory committee, regulations governing the making and withdrawing of nominations, and so on. The provision for elections puts me in mind of what happens in Russia. If the government wants to introduce such regulations, why must we elect an advisory committee? Logically, if the advisory committee is elected, it should control the program and be responsible to its electors. Why should control of the program be vested in Ottawa, in the cabinet? Why should the minister in charge of the Wheat Board try to exercise control of the committee? I cannot accept that provision as logical or reasonable.
If an advisory committee is to be elected, surely it will be composed of members who will want to act in the best interests of prairie grain producers. Why should the governor in council be given ultimate responsibility? The point is one of fundamental importance.
The bill contains other provisions for the making of rules and regulations for the pooling and sale of grain. It will be to the advantage of grain producers if malting barley sales are pooled. Certainly members representing grain producing ridings have received letters from producers complaining about losses in the last two years. On average producers lost about $2,000 per carload; no small amount. If the minister in charge of the Wheat Board had been sufficiently far-sighted, he would have foreseen what could happen. Why should producers on average have lost that $2,000? Grain producers have every right to know.
Sometimes the difference between various grades of barley used for malting is small. There could be little difference between No. 1 feed and 3C grain or barley used for malting. I had a letter from a man who took two carloads of malting barley from the same bin. One was graded 3CW and the other No. 1 feed. To all intents and purposes it was the same grade of grain. He wondered why the grain had been graded differently. He lost about $2,000

on the deal. Clearly, eliminating such discrepancies would be to the benefit of producers.
As the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) suggested earlier, the $2,000 lost might find its way to the pockets of some grain companies. There is a loophole here which ought to be closed. The advisory committee could close it. I do not think it is up to the governor in council to make an order in this regard.
The bill also deals with the pooling and handling of grain. I do not like the provision in the bill for a further tinkering by the governor in council with regard to the cutoff date for the pooling aspect. I do not think it is right, necessary or logical.
Hon. members will recall that during the 1972 election campaign the minister in charge of the Wheat Board did a little tinkering. He had a final payment made prior to the end of the year. This upset a lot of producers because they were used to getting the final payment after the year end and had governed their sales accordingly. This payment upset their whole financial operation. They had to pay income tax on an income they had not anticipated.
This upsetting aspect was not just limited to producers, but to members of the other place. Immediately after that, they brought in a bill stipulating that payments only be made after the beginning of a new calendar year. They were aware of this tinkering by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
The minister is now going to do more tinkering. In this bill there is provision to allow adjustment of the pooling cutoff. It is neither reasonable nor necessary; in fact, the advisory committee could do that. They know when the cutoff should be. If an election is to be held in a year or two, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board could manipulate the final payment to such a degree that it would be of benefit to the government. I do not like this kind of tinkering. It is not fair. I am sure that members opposite do not appreciate that provision the minister is including in this bill.
There is something else that concerns me. The Wheat Board is making provision for an amount in the vicinity of $10 million to provide a storage facility on the west coast. This is made up of producer dollars. We see what is happening in other aspects of industry. Governments provide facilities for the provision or development of manufactured products. We see what is happening in CIDA. Canadian dollars are made available for the promotional activity of manufacturers in this country. I do not see why the federal government cannot undertake this obligation rather than having the Wheat Board undertake it.
There are many things that could be of great benefit to the prairie grain producer. These provisions could be made by the advisory committee. I suggest they will be well versed on the requirements of the industry. More cognizance should be given to them rather than having the control left in the hands of the governor in council.
It is time we realized that all knowledge of the grain industry and the future well-being does not necessarily rest with the government of the day, whether it be with the present government or some future government. More
April 26, 1976

power should be given to the advisory committee because they know the score. They know what is taking place.
I hope that in committee government members and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board will give consideration to the comments that I have made. I do not think the government should take much more control of the industry. A shortcoming of all governments is that they try to build empires. There is no room for any empire building in the production of grain in western Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
We made several amendments to the bill. As a result of some private meetings a consensus was reached on the amendments and the final form of the bill. This is one of the better bills that have been handled since I have been here. We were able to make reasonable progress both at second reading and committee stage.
As hon. members know, the bill deals with tire safety standards and a national tire safety mark. In its original form it provided for the establishment of a record keeping system at the retail level and for a system of inspection to ensure that the records were maintained. I am happy to say that the government recognized the weakness of such a procedure and withdrew that provision in committee. As a matter of fact it was agreed to proceed with the debate on second reading only on the understanding that this provision would be removed.
During the committee stage further changes were made. The term "distributor" was defined along lines more in keeping with those understood by the trade. The bill was further amended to require record-keeping by manufacturers, importers, and others connected with interprovincial trade. Notification of a defective tire was required by certified mail rather than by registered mail as originally written in the bill-we felt this would be an easier, faster, and less costly procedure.
Some amendments were made to Part II of the bill having to do with inspectors and powers of inspectors. As a result we feel the measure now has a reasonable chance of being accepted and implemented broadly across the country by all levels of the trade.
There were other clauses we would have liked to have seen changed. We are still not happy about the definition of safety standards in clause 20. However, we reluctantly accept the testimony of the department's officials that there was no intention to lay down design criteria-nor are they, in fact, capable of designing tires.

speechtext: We know that. They are bureaucrats.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
We know they are not capable of designing anything except a lot of red tape. Hon. members may have noticed recently that a new tire process has been developed in Britain. The tire tread is compressed on to the casing in such a way as to resist cuts in the tread. This promises improved safety and much longer tire life. Such developments are, of course, in the nature of the tire business. It is highly competitive, a high profile business which requires a well organized distribution chain backed by competent service. In the tire business you will find thousands of small businessmen. Both they and the consumers will benefit from this legislation.
When this bill passes and is proclaimed, tires which are being imported into Canada in increasing numbers will come under its control. This is an aspect which concerns us. I do not know whether the legislation we are considering will straighten it out or not, but our tire industry is floundering rather badly right now. The last time I looked at the statistics I found we were producing only about 50 per cent of the radial tires consumed in Canada. If there is any industry in Canada with a potential which is not presently being fulfilled, it is the tire industry. Perhaps

April 26, 1976
Tire Safety Act
when this legislation passes and imported tires are required to go through the inspection process, we may see our own tire dealers become a little more expansionary in their thinking and make added capacity available to serve the domestic market.
Under the bill as presently written, a customer purchasing a tire will have to fill out a card on which the serial number is recorded. This information will be kept by the manufacturer, or importer, or by the interprovincial distributor, and in the event of a tire being found defective they will be required to notify the consumer by certified mail. We think this is how it should be done. The tire industry in general agrees with this procedure. I believe the retail and wholesale dealers across the country are in favour of it and, as I said earlier, the legislation has a reasonable chance of being accepted broadly across the country to the benefit of everyone who purchases tires.
The bill before us started off in the other place and, after lengthy hearings during which some really good evidence was presented, it found its way to this House. Really, it was the evidence presented at the Senate hearings which gave us the idea where to go to get certain changes made. What seemed strange to me was that the government appeared reluctant to accept the testimony presented at the Senate hearings by knowledgeable people.
When it became apparent that the original intent of the government with regard to safety standards was being changed in such a way as to mean the establishment of another great bureaucracy of inspectors to check the records of retail stations, many people who looked at the legislation objectively became angry. Subsequently, to its credit, there was a change of mind; there had been a change of ministers and parliamentary secretaries and we were able to negotiate, one might say.
We wanted to see the legislation passed but we believed the government should remove the record-keeping clause applying to retail tire dealers. As I say, the minister, the parliamentary secretary and the officials saw the wisdom of this approach, and to their credit they made the change which we were proposing. We thought it was a good move. As a matter of fact it was this concession which got the bill going again and prompted us to take it through second reading into committee and pass it there in a relatively short period of time. I hope we can dispose of it this evening so that it can proceed, presumably, to the Senate-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this third reading debate on Bill S-8, which was originally introduced in the other place as

Bill S-3, I think something over two years ago. As the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) has pointed out, we on this side of the House generally support the principle of the bill, though quite frankly the first version presented to the House of Commons, having passed the other place, was a very bad piece of legislation. As the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth said, Bill S-8 represents a vast improvement over that first version with which we were presented.
Had Bill S-3, which is now Bill S-8, been passed in its original form I venture to say that probably one half or three quarters of our independent tire dealers in Canada would have been out of business. Testimony presented to us clearly brought to light the bureaucratic nightmare that this piece of legislation would have caused, and which would have made the whole operation quite unworkable.
In saying this I suppose I am criticizing those in the other place and I am not sure it is parliamentary to do so, but I will take a chance on that anyway.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext: Come on, feel free.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
I think the examination of this legislation in the other place left much to be desired, Mr. Speaker. I think the hon. members of the other place touched the periphery of the contents of this bill, but although some very major objections were raised and talked about, very little action was taken. While the intent of the bill and the principle of the bill are both laudable, I do not think the provisions of the bill would have been properly realized, nor would the objective of safety have been properly achieved had it not been for the close scru-tinization by the members of the House of Commons and the further scrutinization that took place in the transport committee.
I think as originally presented the bill was clearly a classic example of bureaucratic overkill as a result of which the objective of safety would not have been fulfilled. I base this statement in part on testimony presented to the committee, as well as on testimony given in the United States where a similar registration process is currently in existence and where the compliance record is something in the order of 20 to 30 per cent.
Bringing in a piece of legislation that is unworkable, unmanageable, and which will not be complied with will never achieve the purpose for which it is intended. This was the major fault we saw in this piece of legislation. As I said before, these points were clearly identifiable in the testimony examined in the committee and debates in the other place, but our hon. friends in the other place failed to pursue the issues and thereby failed in their attempts to make it a workable piece of legislation. I must say I regret that.
As the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth pointed out, while the bill is far from perfect there have been some major improvements made to it which can be either added to later or improved upon once the legislation comes into force. Certainly the bureaucratic mess that the bill in its original form would have created would not be in the best interests of motor vehicle safety.
As presently framed the bill provides for a form of voluntary registration and for a recall mechanism between
April 26, 1976

manufacturer and end user, which in this case is the final consumer. We think it is in the best interests of consumers to take advantage of the safety provisions in this bill, the recall system, and the registration provisions as prescribed in the regulations. In the event that a consumer purchases a tire from a tire dealer or manufacturer and that particular type of tire becomes defective, the consumer will be notified if a recall is necessary.
As the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth has said, there are some areas in the bill that still give us on this side of the House cause for concern. For example, the notification of a defect as provided for in clause 8 still causes us some concern. We are indeed delighted that the bill has eliminated the necessity for the small tire dealer and retailer to notify the consumer. Now the onus is placed directly upon the manufacturer.
Another criticism that we have relates to clause 8(1) under which, as we read the bill, a manufacturer is guilty of an offence if he fails to give notice of a defect in a tire that is not necessarily sold but which is moved through the merchandizing system of the company. The manufacturer must give notice by certified mail of such defect, otherwise he is guilty of an offence. That is all very well and good when it applies to the end user, the consumer, and we certainly find no fault with that.

speechtext: You want it both ways, do you?

As far as he is concerned, the more regulations the better. He and his colleagues are great advocates of that, and to some extent the government of the day has fallen for that sort of poppycock, which is why we are in the trouble we are in today.

everything.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but these kind of interjections lead one into a discussion of the whole transportation industry, and a lot of our goods are transported on rubber. That is one of our problems. As far as the hon. member is concerned, we should be using steel wheels.

speechtext:
How about square wheels?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
As I was attempting to point out, it is all well and good to engage in a registered mail or certified letter process when notifying the end user, but in the case of notification of the merchandising network, such as the distributors, dealers and sub-dealers, there are perhaps better and more effective methods.
The wording of the bill as it now stands makes it an offence for a manufacturer not to notify by certified mail. In the testimony of the witnesses who appeared before the committee in support of this piece of legislation it was brought out that there may very well be other methods that could prove more effective in the notification process than registered mail. The manufacturer, however, is faced with the possibility of being guilty of an offence if he fails to notify his dealer or distributor by certified mail. All I am saying is that there are other ways and means, such as the telex system. There could be a telephone call within the system. I think there is a differentiation to be made here.
Within the merchandising system we have a different situation than in the case of the consumer or end user. I have no argument or qualms about the provisions which require that the end user be notified by registered mail or certified letter, but there are procedures and methods that could be utilized in notification within the merchandising process. We were given the assurance by the parliamentary secretary and officials of the Department of Transport that such regulations which clarify the notification process will be presented so that the process will not only be effective but also not overly burdensome.
It stands to reason that it would be sheer lunacy to suggest that when a manufacturer ships out 75,000 tires to
3,000	dealers he must send out a certified letter or a letter by registered mail notifying them of a pending difficulty. Surely there are other more appropriate ways and means. It may well be suggested that this is a technicality, but I think it is a matter of some concern to manufacturers.
Our second area of concern is that part which deals with the definition of safety standards. While we appreciate that the definition does conform to the definition in the Motor Vehicle Act, after which this particular piece of legislation is patterned, we were not convinced by the testimony and arguments presented by the parliamentary secretary and the officials that the final test is in performance. We believe the safety standard definitions could in fact regulate the design and construction to such an extent that this may well affect future advancement in the manufacture and production of tires. The Michelin people, for example, in a letter which was submitted to the committee on November 19, stated:
We feel that the definition of "Safety Standards" ... should not be worded in a manner which could considerably restrict future design possibilities and innovations. "Safety Standards" should mean actual performance standards and all marking requirements specifically. We feel that design and construction of a tire, as we would define those words, are such that they should be left specifically to the manufacturer.
In addition, it is pointed out in a letter to myself from the Michelin people as follows:
We would like to point out in more general terms, to yourself, that in establishing new performance standards, which are in essence minimum standards, that they can have quite the reverse effect to that

April 26, 1976
Tire Safety Act
desired, instead of bringing up the standards of the lesser grades of a product it can encourage design down to those minimum standards.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext: What is the date of the letter?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
That date of that letter is March 19, 1976, and I thank the hon. member for drawing that to my attention because I think it is a very pertinent and logical argument.
We do not want to bring forward a bill that would provide for minimum safety standards. What we want to do is encourage optimum standards in respect of automobile tires, whether that be safety and/or performance.
The suggestion here by the Michelin people is that the current definition in the bill establishes a minimum standard which could in fact encourage the tire manufacturers to design downward rather than upward. This is something that may well be a valid consideration. Quite frankly I think the definition could have been dressed up considerably. I do not believe it is the intention of the ministry to dictate design and construction to automobile tire manufacturers. That being the case, this should not be included in the bill.
Safety standards as now defined at page 2 of the bill mean standards regulating the design, construction or function of a motor vehicle tire for the purpose of protecting persons against personal injury, impairment of health, or death.
Quite frankly we believe the key here is performance rather than design and construction. It really does not matter what sort of formula is used in the fabricating of a tire as long as it is safe, performs properly, and meets these standards. We think we can live with that. However, in the opinion of the minister and his representatives, that was not a valid argument. I simply reiterate that we have some reservations about that aspect of the bill.
The other area about which we have some concern is the power of the inspectors. Here again we may be overly concerned, but I feel I must place on the record some of the concerns that have been advanced by the Michelin tire people. I do not have any association with the Michelin people, but I do know, as I am sure many of my colleagues do, that they have set optimum standards in terms of tires and tire safety. Therefore I value the points they have advanced in respect of this particular piece of legislation. They are somewhat concerned about the wording of the section as it relates to the design and construction, but more so in terms of clause 11 as it now stands.
I refer to a letter directed to the Committee on Transportation and Communications dated March 24, 1976. It states:
With clause 11 as it stands now, there is no limitation of power of the inspectors, therefore an inspector can enter any Canadian tire manufacturing facility, photocopy all documents to his liking, freeze all movement of products for a period of 90 or more days and walk away.
The consequences are easy to imagine: work methods and procedures, trade secrets as well as production capacities available to all government employees, thus the Canadian public. Frozen movement of the products will stop production lines causing massive lay-offs and therefore economic hardship to the affected company and to the employees of that company.
It may seem an exaggeration, but with the clause 11 of the act as it is worded now, this is possible and it is in the hands of one inspector who,

according to clause 11 (1), may reasonably believe there is any motor vehicle tire of a class etc.
Gentlemen, we appeal to you, as members of the standing committee, to reconsider the powers of the inspector, to seek assurance that only when an actual safety related problem is evident, is the inspector entitled to the search and seizure powers conferred by this act.
Perhaps that may be a bit of over-exaggeration but nonetheless I think it draws attention to the very wide powers the inspectors have under the provisions of this bill.
With those reservations, Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in seeing this bill move forward because I believe it is a bill which clearly all Canadians would support. We on this side of the House support it. We are grateful to members on the government side for accepting some of our suggestions and for dealing in a very serious and sincere way with the reservations we advanced.
Along with my good friend from Halton-Wentworth I wish to pay a tribute to the parliamentary secretary, who indeed has been very helpful in respect of this bill.
In closing I want to say this piece of legislation has one glaring loophole in that it fails to recognize the retread tire. As I pointed out in my initial remarks, this bill has been before the House for over two years. During that time in the testimony that was advanced we were led to believe there would be a code of standards brought forward by the government relating to the safety standards of retreads. It is very discouraging to note that there has not been any progress in this particular area.
While there has been some concern by the government about moving this bill forward, there has been absolutely no progress, so far as we are aware, concerning the question of the retread tire. I think the Ministry of Transport and the government have been derelict in providing leadership to bring together the retreaders and manufacturers in the kind of association that would provide the kind of standards which should govern the sale of retread tires across the country.
It seems to me that a retreaded tire should pass a performance test just the same as a brand new tire. I am told that in the United States a retreader is responsible for maintaining the same standards as those required for a new tire. I think that is a very simple standard. During this two year interval in which we have focused attention on the question of tire safety I think it would have behooved the government and the Ministry of Transport to have come forward and established a proper code or a proper standard governing the sale of retreaded tires.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext: I wish you would make up your mind.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
While we welcome this particular bill as it applies to new tires, we must say very simply that we regret there has been little or no initiative taken in the area of retread tires. My friend said that he wished I would make up my mind. I am as interested as he is in the safety of tires. He does not have a monopoly on the question of safety. I happen to know a little more about the tire business than he. He may be a little jealous. I can assure him that I am as concerned about retread tires as I am about new tires, both of which are being sold very readily on today's market.
April 26, 1976

In the two years that this bill has been before the House one would have considered that the government, particularly this minister and his very effervescent and knowledgeable parliamentary secretary, before engaging in an attempt to sell us on this measure would have come forth with some positive recommendation in the area of retread tires. I hope that now we are giving them the satisfaction of the passage of this bill they will not delay too long in coming forward and perhaps orchestrating the kind of a system which should govern the sale of retread tires in this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH SAFETY STANDARDS FOR TIRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased this evening to see that on this occasion we are back before the House of Commons once again at the report stage of Bill S-8 to consider a number of amendments that have been proposed and approved by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I hope this indicates that the House will give this bill its approval very shortly. In this connection I am very pleased to have heard the remarks of the hon. members who spoke just before me.
I want to express a word of thanks to the members of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications and also to the witnesses who appeared before that committee in the course of our deliberations. I should like to thank the committee members for their co-operation in the thorough and fair consideration which I believe has resulted in some improvements to the bill. I should like to commend as well the very real contribution to this bill by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski).
Dealing very briefly at the outset with the concluding comments of my friend from Vegreville, I want to assure him sincerely that the issue to which he referred, the matter of retread tires, is not one which has escaped the attention or the concern of the government. Indeed we share the concern he expressed this evening. I assure him work is going forward in that particular area, and I hope we may be able soon to contend with the problem which he outlined earlier this evening.
The history of this particular piece of legislation I think is pretty well understood. It was introduced in the Senate in its original form two years ago as Bill S-3. After examination by the Senate Standing Committee on Transport and Communications and subsequent approval by the Senate, the bill unfortunately expired on the order paper of the House of Commons. It was re-introduced and passed by the other place in October, 1974, as Bill S-8. First reading was given to Bill S-8 in this House in October, 1974, and second reading was completed on March 4, 1976. Our Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has given careful study to the bill and has approved a number of amendments which I believe have improved this piece of legislation, as I said earlier.
The general objectives of the Motor Vehicle Tire Safety Act have not changed in the course of the last couple of years of work. This bill, when passed, will lead to increased safety of Canadian motorists and will prevent unfair competition for Canadian tire manufacturing plants.
Tire Safety Act
During discussion of this bill, both at second reading and in the standing committee, the need for such a bill has been questioned. In particular there has been some suggestion that the implementation of this legislation will not contribute greatly to road safety. On the other hand, I believe many of the comments made during second reading related to the very real concern that many of us have about the quality and safety of the tires that are offered for sale in this country.
The testimony that many of us had the opportunity to hear in the committee demonstrated that Canadian manufacturers are indeed doing an excellent job in producing first class tires for the Canadian consumer. However, there was also testimony that indicated that on occasion defective tires do get produced and do result in serious road accidents. It is the objective of this bill to see that these occasions are rare and that when they do occur that motorists have the opportunity of being notified in advance of the defects so that they may avoid driving their cars on potentially dangerous tires.
The passage of this bill will also enhance federal-provincial co-operation by assisting the provinces in overcoming problems involving the control of tire safety at the point of retail sale.
The main provisions of this legislation probably bear repeating and emphasizing at this time. The bill will establish the authority for the governor in council to prescribe safety standards for minimum tire safety requirements. These standards will be established for new tires manufactured in Canada and for all tires imported into this country. The bill establishes a national tire safety mark and, by use of the mark, tire manufacturers will be certifying that they comply with the prescribed safety standards.
Manufacturers and distributors will be prohibited from exporting or from sending or carrying from one province to another motor vehicle tires to which the national safety mark has not been applied. Manufacturers and importers will be required to give notice of any safety related tire defects of which they become aware. The bill establishes the method by which this notice must be given.
As has been mentioned earlier in the House this evening, the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has given careful consideration to the problems this bill might have created for small distributors and dealers. As was mentioned during the second reading, it was never the government's intention to require dealers to maintain a detailed record system of their tire sales, nor was there any intention to establish a large staff of inspectors to ensure that the act was being complied with at the small distributor and dealer level. For this reason two main amendments were proposed, one establishing a record system in which consumers could have their names recorded if they so desired, and a second providing that inspectors already designated under the Motor Vehicle Safety Act be designated as inspectors under this act.
The committee, as a result of consultation, settled on a number of amendments which will limit certain responsibilities under the act to manufacturers, importers, and only those distributors who are in the business of selling in more than one province or country; the responsibility for giving notice of safety related defects, as a result of these

April 26, 1976
Tire Safety Act
amendments, has been clearly left to the manufacturers and importers.
I think that as hon. members go through this legislation and compare the bill which is before the House this evening with the one which was referred to the committee some weeks ago they will find that a number of amendments have been made to it. For the information of those hon. members who would like to follow the course of this legislation I would point out that the most significant of these amendments are to clauses 2, 4, 5, and 7, and probably the most important is to clause 8.
The proposed change to clause 8 will result in the distributors having no responsibility for notifying subsequent tire purchasers of safety related defects. Instead this responsibility will lie entirely with the manufacturers or importers. Therefore the consumer will still be assured that he will be notified of a defect if he has his name recorded with the manufacturer or importer. However, distributors and dealers will not be responsible for maintaining a record of tire purchasers.
Clause 8(2)(a) is also to be amended so that certified mail may be used rather than registered mail in notifying purchasers of safety related defects.
Clause 10 is also a clause to which hon. members may wish to refer to see some of the work of the standing committee. Clause 11 was another such clause. In view of the lateness of the hour I will confine my concluding remarks to clause 11, and be brief with respect to it.
The proposed amendment to clause 11 will ensure that inspectors do not have a completely free run of a manufacturer's premises. Inspectors will be able to inspect tires at the point of manufacture. However, they will only be able to inspect completed tires that are to be offered for sale. Therefore they will not be involved with experimental or developmental tires. This possibility concerned the industry and, as the House has heard, it concerns hon. members opposite as well, and I believe these amendments will satisfy the industry that the inspectors will only be concerned with tires that will find their way into the market place.
I am satisfied that these amendments do not compromise the original objectives of the bill. In fact I believe they will strengthen the bill by making it more practical, and by more clearly defining the responsibilities of manufacturers, importers, and distributors. In view of all this I believe that at this time Bill S-8 is worthy of the support of all parties in this House.

Mr. Speaker, in the one minute left I only want to say that while we agree that this legislation should be passed we think it is window dressing. In spite of all the nit picking by the official opposition and the protestations by the government it will not guarantee proper safety and performance.
I would like to remind the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), who said he knows so much about the tire business, that I too dealt with it for about eight years and I know that every reputable small businessman and retailer keeps accurate records of the serial numbers, kinds, makes, and sizes of tires, and that whatever fears he might have had have nothing to do with safety and performance and the protection of the public.

The legislation can well be passed tonight but it will make little difference in experience in the next few years because both the government and the official opposition have chickened out and have not done something really important about tire safety.

SUPPLY AND SERVICES-LOCKHEED CONTRACT-ARRANGEMENTS FOR INTERIM FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without upsetting any delicate arrangements that may be about to be culminated with respect to the replacement of the Argus or interfering with it because all of us, particularly on this side, are very concerned that Maritime Command get a replacement, I wish to say that there is no question that we continue to agree that that replacement should be the Orion. However, we continue to have some very grave concern about mismanagement and very bad handling with respect to the details of the contract, and my purpose tonight is to try to touch on three questions which I raised shortly prior to the Easter recess with respect to perhaps a narrow aspect of this situation. They have to do with the authority or the absence of authority for the spending of any moneys by the Department of National Defence or on behalf of National Defence by the Department of Supply and Services, or the authorizing by Supply and Services of the expenditures of any funds prior to the establishment of a contract.
I think it would serve the understanding of Canadians, particularly hon. members on this side of the House, quite substantially if we were to understand a little more about the background for proceeding in the absence of a contract,
April 26, 1976

and particularly for proceeding when there was reason to believe that the contract would give rise to some considerable problems.
As I indicated, I do not particularly want to make comments or observations this evening which would jeopardize the situation as we now have it. I think we would be reassured if the parliamentary secretary could indicate to us tonight one or two things; first, if he could touch on the nature of the authority and from whence it came with respect to expenditures which were made in the absence of a contract; second, if he could give us some indication with respect to timing, because I understand that, perhaps even more than the Department of National Defence, the Department of Supply and Services continues to be very closely and deeply involved in this contract; third, we would appreciate hearing tonight a reiteration of the assurance that in connection with any announcement either the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) or the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) might again undertake immediately to table the contract and that the minister will refer that contract to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence so that the members of that committee and Canadians in general will have some understanding of the contract and some understanding of just what it is we are getting into.
Finally, there is a fourth area. I recognize that this falls a little closer into the area of1 policy which would be more clearly national defence, but in this interim period has any consideration been given by the ministry, by the Treasury benches, or by the Department of National Defence to proceeding with the development and work up of a contract which would effectively reduce, change or alter the form of the replacement equipment? What I am getting at is whether there has been any consideration given by the Treasury Board to charging other user departments a portion of the capital cost of the Orion so that the cost to the Department of National Defence will not be in the order of $60 million to $70 million, or possibly even $75 million or $80 million, but rather more in the order of $30 million. It seems unreasonable that the Department of National Defence should be asked to pay twice as much for an aircraft in terms of its capital cost when other government departments will utilize to an extensive degree the capacities and capabilities of this aircraft.
Those are the four areas upon which I should like the parliamentary secretary to touch. I think we would be enlightened and grateful, and I appreciate his being here this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-LOCKHEED CONTRACT-ARRANGEMENTS FOR INTERIM FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to answer the hon. member's questions in three minutes. I shall begin by speaking on the interim financing arrangements for the Lockheed contract.
Regarding the interim financing for the Lockheed contract, it must be recognized that, as the contracting agency for most government departments, the Department of Supply and Services is not directly responsible for the provision of program funds to support the requirements of customers. Officers of the department and, particularly, the DSS members of the LRPA joint project office have been actively assisting the Department of National
Adjournment Debate
Defence in endeavours to resolve the DND cash shortfall in the early years of the program.
The matter has not been finalized as of this date and we have been requested to enter into an option arrangement with Lockheed whereby the price, schedules, and industrial benefits for the LRPA acquisition would be protected through April, 1976. This afternoon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) said that he hoped to be in a position to make an announcement soon.
Let me now say a word with regard to the authority to spend the money. The cabinet initially approved the selection of the Lockheed P3 LRPA aircraft on November 27, 1975, and approval to contract was issued by Treasury Board on December 2, 1975. On this basis a conditional acceptance of Lockheed's offer which otherwise would have expired was issued in order to preserve the integrity of the offer, including price and Canadian industrial benefits. The same approval process has been followed in the case of the recently negotiated option to extend the original conditions, price, and benefits to April 30, 1976.
The hon. member also raised another question concerning the P3 LRPA. The aircraft is essentially configured to meet specific defence requirements, although certain items of surveillance equipment can also be utilized for non-military purposes such as pollution protection, ice reconnaissance and so on. During the definition phase a policy decision was made not to ask other departments to contribute to capital costs. However, new tasks could arise in future and cost recovery principles may apply when the aircraft are used on missions dedicated for other departments.
The Minister of National Defence has said on several occasions that negotiations taking place between the Lockheed company and the banks are going ahead in a constructive way. Earlier today, replying to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), the minister said that negotiations are in the final stages and an announcement will be made shortly. There is no change from the initially expressed intention of the Department of National Defence to proceed with the contract for the Lockheed long-range patrol aircraft which is to replace the Argus.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-PICKERING-PLANS FOR USE OF LAND IN VIEW OF ABANDONMENT OF CONSTRUCTION PLANS
AIRPORTS-PICKERING-PLANS FOR USE OF LAND IN VIEW OF ABANDONMENT OF CONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I am raising tonight is connected with the question I directed initially to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on April 7.1 then directed it to the acting Minister of Transport, who was then the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey); he, in turn, referred the question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goo-dale) who said, as reported at page 12580 of Hansard, ".... I will certainly bring the question to the attention of the minister."
My question concerned Pickering. I simply asked if the government intended to return the Pickering area lands to previous owners and, if not, what exactly did the government propose to do with those lands. I asked the question even though in the last two or three years 84 oral questions concerning Pickering have been directed to the government. There is still tremendous doubt on what the govern-

April 26, 1976
Adjournment Debate
ment's decision is to be on this unfortunately conceived project.
I asked my question because current statistics show that air travel in Canada and in many other parts of the world has, so to speak, "plateau-ed out." The government's repeated statements that somehow Malton will become overcrowded do not appear to be backed up by existing statistics. I would also point out that another tragedy, Mirabel, is perhaps becoming the most costly white elephant in the world. I think that we, as members of this House, have to accept the responsibility of ensuring that the government, in spite of itself, does not create a still more costly white elephant than Mirabel is at the present time.
I say this because when we review both the answers to written questions on this subject and to oral questions, we find there is a great discrepancy among the ministers who respond to the questions. For example, as long ago as May 1, 1974, in answer to a written question, the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of transport stated that the total cost, expressed in 1973 dollars, of Pickering would be $434,429,000. That seems to have been the high admitted cost of Pickering. Ever since, ministers one after another have played down the total cost of this concept, sometimes stating it might be about $200 million that is committed.
We know from the current estimates that the government is still proposing to spend money on Pickering in spite of the fact it is clear the majority of those in the Toronto area do not want this airport. It is clear the Ontario government has asked that the airport be delayed.
In short, my question of April 7 was simply one of clarification; would the present administration now tell us what it proposes to do with these lands, not only the expropriated lands, but the noise lands that it has so unfairly caused to be frozen surrounding the Pickering airport site?
Last fall my colleague from Blind River asked what it proposed to do with the farm land it had expropriated. At that time the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) indicated the government was going to endeavour to get farmers to come in and farm it while it waited for the actual development of Pickering. Hopefully the answer tonight will give some further knowledge. Has it in fact rented the land for farm purposes? Spring is here. It is important that those
18,000	acres be devoted as much as possible to agricultural production.
Historical sites are involved. What is the government's position? Has it finally accepted that there are certain significant historical sites there that should not be permanently destroyed, as was apparently the original intention of the present administration?
I would also like to point out that there has been much talk about the Gibson report. When you review the questions in this House, there was great anxiety on the part of the members as to the position of that inquiry. Subsequently there was a general feeling that the Gibson report gave fairly good evidence that the present administration should not continue with the project as originally intended. What is the attitude of the present administration? Does it intend to proceed in spite of the Gibson report, and

in spite of the attitude of the Ontario government that the project should not be allowed to continue?
It is time that the present administration gave us a candid answer. I hope it will come to its senses and say that it has agreed to abandon the project, it was an unfortunate concept in the beginning, it was something of a civil service dream that it finally realizes is not needed, and that the money that would be spent on Pickering will be spent on a much more worth-while cause than was originally proposed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-PICKERING-PLANS FOR USE OF LAND IN VIEW OF ABANDONMENT OF CONSTRUCTION PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond this evening to my friend, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I believe this is the first opportunity that I have had during a late show proceeding in this House to discuss an issue with the hon. gentleman. I take the gist of his question to be this: what plans does the Government of Canada have with respect to the land involved in the Pickering airport site?
While final statistics are not yet available, there appears to have been little or no growth in Toronto's air traffic during 1975, but this in itself is not sufficient reason to throw away for all time the option for the people of the Toronto area ultimately to establish airport facilities at the Pickering site. There have also been slowdowns in the past, but the hard lesson that must be learned in the art of forecasting demand for airport facilities is that one cannot decide major long term options on the basis of short term fluctuations in traffic.
We have reason to believe that the 1975 air traffic pattern is just that, a short term fluctuation in what would still appear to be an over-all upward trend, at least in the foreseeable future. This growth plateau is not surprising when one considers economic conditions in 1975 and the unusually high rate of growth between 1971 and 1974; Toronto traffic increased 56 per cent over those three years in comparison with total United States traffic growth of about 20 per cent in the same period.
On the likely basis then that traffic will increase again, it remains the view of the federal government that a second airport may well be needed in the Toronto area. For this reason it is our intention to retain the option for the people of Toronto of providing needed airport facilities at some time in the future. Whether facilities are needed in 1980 or 1985 does not alter the long term need. The government cannot wilfully commit itself to a course of action such as has been suggested, one which would inevitably mean the loss of all flexibility in meeting future needs.
At present Toronto handles about 25 per cent of the nation's air traffic, and we feel that failure to provide adequate facilities in the area would ultimately hamper Toronto's ability to compete effectively on an economic basis with other cities in North America. In the meantime the land at Pickering will be retained by the federal government and is being put to productive use through leasing of the properties for farming.
As most people are now aware, at the time of expropriation over 50 per cent of the airport site was owned by speculative interests and only about 10,500 acres of the
18,000	total acres were being actively farmed. The production yield from the site was considerably below the aver-
April 26, 1976

age for similar agricultural land elsewhere in Ontario. Since the expropriation we have attempted to maximize the use of the land by leasing all the rentable residential and farm property. At present some 14,000 acres are devoted to farming, an increase of over 33 per cent since the land was acquired. The government has committed itself to developing a long term program to maximize agricultural production on the site, even in the event airport facilities are developed.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member agrees that the only responsible course of action is the one we are presently following. It allows adequate flexibility in the long term while making the best use of present facilities in the short term. At the same time, the agricultural resources now in the government's charge at the Pickering site are being productively managed to the advantage of the Toronto area.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CAMBODIA-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED VIOLATIONS OF HUMAN RIGHTS-SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF AID
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CAMBODIA-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED VIOLATIONS OF HUMAN RIGHTS-SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to expand this evening on a question I first asked on March 18, and continued to repeat as lately as April 7. In so doing I wish to quote from the Sunday Times, a British newspaper, of April 18, a date subsequent to my last raising of this subject. I propose to quote from an article by Jon Swain, named "Journalist of the Year" in the 1975 British press awards for his despatches on the fall of Cambodia to the Communists. He has now returned to the borders of that country to report on the tragic and profound revolution forced on its people in just one year. He says:
If any country deserves the world's compassion and interest it is Cambodia.
Nevertheless, the attempts made by myself and others in this House to obtain any sort of response when we raise this subject have been met with precious little interest and, certainly, with no compassion.
Writing about this particular revolution, Mr. Swain says:
It is now clear that this has obliterated what little progress had been made in the past hundred years and destroyed an ancient civilization which had stayed intact for centuries.
He goes on to say:
But it has been the Khmer Rouge, forcing a uniquely painful brand of communism on to a bewildered, demoralized peasantry at the point of a gun, that has prolonged and darkened the tragedy.
Further he says:
Probably the world will never know how many Cambodians have died or had their lives irreparably broken by the Khmer Rouge's rush to force a new society ...
Other reports have been bold enough to estimate the dead to be as high as 600,000. The government's hesitancy to display any interest in this area is to me very strange. I can recall during the twenty-seventh parliament we were constantly sending special missions to Hanoi, which is not all that far from Phnom Penh in Cambodia, in an endeavour to lessen hostilities. No amount of American bombing or danger could keep us out of Hanoi at that time.
Adjournment Debate
We found a way to overcome every obstacle and to send our special representatives to Hanoi.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we know that the government, which oddly enough does not even have a parliamentary secretary in the House at the moment to respond to my question, is prepared to make a big gesture in responding to conditions in some other parts of the world. We have seen in the last few weeks threats to cut off federal assistance to the Olympics for the Handicapped because a South African team, which was integrated, was permitted to enter that competition. The action of the federal government at that moment was swift and sure. I find it a strange double standard.
I made inquiries whether this country was prepared to send a special mission to Cambodia to ascertain what had happened in that country. I received no response. I inquired whether our aid to the Khmer Republic had been cut off and was told there was no aid. This was reassuring because in 1972 our aid amounted to $30,000, in 1973 to $50,000, and in 1974 to $100,000. I notice the parliamentary secretary has now arrived so perhaps I can have an answer to my questions.
If this accelerated rate in the growth of aid to the Khmer Republic has been cut off, I wonder when it was cut off and what was the motive. Was it their unilateral action, or was it as a protest by this country against the situation developing in that part of the world once the communist Khmer regime had taken over? I admit the amounts spent were small, but was there no residue of good will in that country? Cannot we find among the representatives in that area over the years someone we could send to that country to plead for some respect of human life and to give an indication of our interest in and compassion for that extremely troubled land?

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-CAMBODIA-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON ALLEGED VIOLATIONS OF HUMAN RIGHTS-SUGGESTED WITHDRAWAL OF AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Okanagan Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) has spoken on several occasions about the question of aid to Cambodia. He mentioned previously that the United States deemed it timely to withdraw their aid. Now, I fail to see the relevancy of this statement to Canada. In fact, this country no longer provides assistance to Cambodia since April 1975 and no aid program is being considered for the time being. No Canadian diplomat is accredited with the Cambodian government and the contacts we have with the few Cambodian diplomats posted abroad are very casual.
I think he will remember that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and myself have declared on several occasions that it was extremely difficult to obtain reliable information on what is going on in Cambodia at the moment. None of our allies has any diplomat stationed in Phom Penh and reporters have no access to the country. According to our information, chances are very remote that this situation will change in a forseeable future because the Cambodian regime has clearly indicated that it is not interested in receiving diplomatic missions from countries that recognized the former regime of General Lon Nol, of which Canada was.
Their attitude is the same with regard to international agencies which managed assistance programs under the

April 26, 1976
Adjournment Debate
former regime. Their representatives were expelled from Cambodia at the same time as all other foreigners in the spring of 1975. Even the International Red Cross, which tried to reestablish ties with its Cambodian branch, has had no success to date. The policy of isolationism, devoid of any practical concessions, of the present Cambodian government makes it therefore extremely difficult for the Canadian government to attempt to get information on the development of events in that country.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, to my mind, there is little probability that the United Nations will be asked to
look into the matter of the rights of the people and all other related matters unless individuals or non-governmental groups, with a first hand and reliable knowledge of recent events in Cambodia, bring forth directly a grievance for violation of human rights before the agency of the General Assembly of the UN entrusted with that type of problem, as that is the procedure that must be followed when human rights are violated, or in cases of torture, which cases have repeatedly been reported as occurring in Cambodia.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.29 p.m.
